en: The *Mānameyodaya* composed by Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa (a Kerala work on Pūrva-mīmāṃsā):
The Section on the Means of Valid Cognition (*Pramāṇapariccheda*).

May this certain "Calf of Gopāla" serve as a boat for us— wise ones who wish to lead even children across the ocean of the Teacher’s thought, which is the examination of direct perception (*pratyakṣaparīkṣā*). (1)

The existence of entities is twofold, through the distinction between the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge; therefore, we shall explain both of these according to the path of the illustrious Kumārila.
In this context, the instrument of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is simply the means of producing valid knowledge (pramākaraṇa), just as in the case of the position of the logicians (tarkapakṣa).
Furthermore, valid knowledge (pramā) is distinguished solely as the cognition of an object whose true nature was previously unknown. ||3||

By the term "unknown" (*ajñāta*) here, there is the exclusion of recollection (*smṛti*) and restatement (*anuvāda*), both of which have known objects. Regarding this, the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) in restatements is not accepted by the Logicians (*tārkika*) and others. We, however, say: for a restatement brings about no distinction whatsoever from a prior cognition, whether in the determination of an object or in practical usage (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, because there is an absence of a specific result (*phala-viśeṣa*), and since the acceptance of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is for the sake of a result, even a restatement must be excluded, just like recollection and the like.

Surely, if only the apprehension of the unknown constitutes validity (*prāmāṇya*), then in a series of successive cognitions such as "this is a jar, this is a jar," the second and subsequent cognitions would lack validity. Not so. For even there, because each subsequent cognition apprehends a portion of time that was previously unknown—namely, the existence of the jar and so forth at a later moment, which was not grasped by the preceding cognition—the validity remains. But one might object: since the distinction between times is merely conditional (*aupādhika*), it must be stated by what condition these portions of time are delimited and apprehended here. It is said in reply:

Because the manifestations (*prākaṭya*) determined by each preceding cognition persist until the final subsequent cognition, there is an apprehension of the portions of time delimited by them at each respective stage. Nor should it be argued that because the various manifestations are subtle, the temporal divisions delimited by them are likewise too subtle to be perceived; for if they were so subtle, it would follow that one would have the illusion of simultaneity—such as "the jar is perceived all at once"—just as when a hundred lotus petals are pierced simultaneously by a needle.

In this case, however, because there is a sequential cognition of "this" and "that" again and again, established as having the nature of a continuous stream (*dhārāvāhika*), there is indeed a contradiction in the conceit of simultaneity. Therefore, there is no subtlety in the differences of manifestation (*prākaṭya*) or the differences of time. If it is objected: "Since manifestation itself does not exist and time is not perceptible, how can parts of time be understood?", we reply: No, for both of those will be proven later. By the word *tattva* (reality), erroneous cognitions such as delusion and doubt are excluded.

Regarding this, the Prābhākaras assert that the term "tattva" (truth) is redundant because there is no such thing as false knowledge (*ayathārthajñāna*). Their view is as follows: in the cognition "this is silver," the piece of mother-of-pearl is perceived as "this" without its specific features being grasped; meanwhile, "silver" is merely remembered. Due to the non-apprehension of the difference between these two, one who seeks silver acts toward the object present before them, but it is not the case that the piece of mother-of-pearl appears as having the nature of silver.

Since it is a rule that every cognition causes activity only toward its own object, if the cognition of silver did not have "this" (*idam*) as its object, activity toward it would not be established; likewise, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) expressed as "this very thing is silver" would not be established without the perception of non-difference between the two. This [objection] should be refuted by such lines of reasoning. Therefore, because cognitions such as error—which consist of apprehending something otherwise—do exist, the word *tattva* (reality) is used for the purpose of excluding them.

Thus, it is established that the sense-organ contacts and so forth possess the status of *pramāṇa* (means of valid cognition) by virtue of being the instruments (*karaṇa*) for *pramā*, which consists in the apprehension of an object whose true nature was previously unknown. Furthermore, since the word *pramā* is used here figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to denote its effect—namely, *prākaṭya* (manifestation)—they maintain that knowledge (*jñāna*) also possesses the status of *pramāṇa* by being the instrument for the *pramā* that takes the form of *prākaṭya*. On this basis, we are celebrated as proponents of the theory that the result [itself] is the means of valid cognition (*phala-pramāṇavādin*). The logicians (*tārkika*), however, define it as: "The instrument of valid cognition is *pramāṇa*."

They define valid cognition (*pramā*) as "experience that accords with reality," and they characterize experience as "cognition distinct from memory. This definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*), because it fails to exclude restatement (*anuvāda*), which lacks validity, and because no term is present here to exclude it. The Prābhākaras maintain: "Valid cognition is experience; and experience is consciousness distinct from memory. This too is over-extensive, because it applies to errors (*bhrama*) and the like, since these are also distinct from memory.

Furthermore, according to their view, even in all cognitions, the triad—the self, the nature of the cognition itself, and the object—is manifested. Moreover, they maintain that in every case, the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) and direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*) belongs to both the self and its own nature. Consequently, if only cognition distinct from memory were considered a means of valid cognition, then memory would lack validity regarding the self and its own nature; thus, there is also the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*). The Buddhists hold that "valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge, and non-contradiction consists in the capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*)."

In that case, inference would lack validity because it lacks causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*) regarding objects that are past or future; whereas memory might possess validity because it occasionally possesses causal efficacy.

Therefore, for us, a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is simply that which brings about the cognition of an object whose true nature (*tattva*) was previously unknown. Its specific varieties are explained subsequently. (4)
Perception, inference, verbal testimony, as well as comparison, presumptive testimony, and non-existence—these are the six means of valid cognition for those like me. (5)
The Cārvākas maintain one [pramāṇa]; the Buddhists and Vaiśeṣikas, as well as Bhāsarvajña, maintain two; the Sāṅkhyas maintain three; Udayana and others maintain four;
the Prābhākaras maintain five; and we, the knowers of Vedānta, maintain six.
The six Paurāṇikas, however, declared it to be eightfold, on account of its connection with the accounts of origins and traditional history.

Among these, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arising from the contact of the sense organs with their objects is perception (*pratyakṣa*). What, then, are the sense organs? It is said: there are six sense organs—namely, the tongue, nose, skin, ear, and the mind (*manas*). The "eye" is the light situated within the pupil; the "tongue" is the watery element at the tip of the tongue; the "nose" is a portion of earth located in the nostrils; the "skin" consists of particles of air spread throughout the entire body; the "ear" is the space within the cavity of the ear; and the "mind," however, is all-pervading, yet it brings about its effects within the body.

In that regard, since it must be established in a general sense that there must be some cause for the cognition of form (*rūpa*), and because it is observed that light such as that of a lamp is indeed the cause of the cognition of form, the eye is postulated as being composed of fire (*taijasa*). Likewise, when postulating a cause for the cognition of taste (*rasa*), since the capacity to manifest taste is seen only in water in the case of dry objects, the tongue is postulated as being composed of water (*āpya*).

Thus, since it is observed that an ointment made of sandalwood and neem—which are both earthy—manifests their respective fragrances, the olfactory organ, which is postulated as the manifestor of fragrance, is composed of earth. Furthermore, since it is observed that the breeze from a fan manifests the touch of water clinging to the body, the tactile organ (*tvagindriya*), which perceives touch, is composed of air. As for the auditory organ (*śrotra*), which is postulated as the grasper of sound, its nature is that of space (*ākāśa*) by the process of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).

Indeed, it is not observed that the eye and other [senses] are produced from the commencement of other [elements], because fire (*tejas*) and the others do not originate other senses; therefore, they do not possess the nature of the ear. Furthermore, since it is observed that the external sense organs consist of the elements (*bhūta*), it follows that the ear must consist of the remaining element called space (*ākāśa*). However, some argue that because sound is a quality (*guṇa*) of space, the ear, which perceives it, must consist of space. That is incorrect, as it is impossible for it to be a quality of that [space].

The mind (*manas*), however, is postulated as the sense organ that serves as the means for the direct perception of pleasure and so forth. Its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) is established; nevertheless, it functions as a sense organ only when delimited by the body, and thus it performs its operations only within that specific region. Even in the cognition of color and other such objects, it operates entirely dependent upon the eyes and other [senses]; likewise, in inference and other forms of knowledge, it relies on the presence of the logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth—such is the established position.

In this regard, since there is a dispute concerning the fact that the eye and the ear function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*), their status as external sense organs—just like the skin and others—must establish that they too function by reaching their objects. Consequently, because the eye perceives vast objects such as mountains, its nature as light (*tejas*) must be accepted as having an extremely subtle dimension (*pṛthvagatva*). Likewise, since one perceives very distant objects such as Saturn at the very moment of opening the eyes, it must be postulated that the external light situated within the body becomes unified with [the visual organ] at the very time of its exit.

Nor does it follow that the Gaṅgā would be visible even from Kerala, because external light pervades everything; for its visibility is restricted by the fact that it becomes unified [with the eye] only through a specific portion of light not obstructed by unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*). Logicians, however, attempt to account for this distant vision on the basis of an extraordinary velocity. We have disregarded their position, as the sudden perception of planets such as Śanaiścara, despite being separated by infinite *yojanas*, cannot be explained by velocity alone.

Furthermore, since these [objects], beginning with the eye, are not perceived through direct perception because their color and touch are unmanifest, the sense organs are established [as distinct entities]. Contact (*sannikarṣa*), however, is of two kinds: conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and identity-in-what-is-conjoined (*saṃyuktatādātmya*). Among these, earth, water, and fire are apprehended by the eyes and the tactile organ through conjunction; air is apprehended through conjunction with the tactile organ; direction, ether, and darkness through conjunction with the eyes; sound through conjunction with the auditory organ; and the self through conjunction with the mind.

In this context, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) arises from the contact of the soul with the mind, even though both are all-pervading (*vibhu*). As for time (*kāla*), since it will be explained that the cognition of "simultaneity" and so forth has time as its object and is produced by a sense organ, and because that [time] is produced by all the sense organs, it is apprehended through conjunction with all the sense organs. However, when there is the apprehension of universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*karman*)—which are of the same nature as those aforementioned substances such as earth—that have come into conjunction with the eyes and other senses, then the means of contact (*sannikarṣa*) is "identity with the conjoined" (*saṃyuktatādātmya*). As it has been said:
"For us, the identity of color and the rest with the substance in which they reside is precisely what constitutes [the contact]."
"Therefore, there is no desire for another type of relation as the cause of cognition.

When, however, there is the apprehension of universals, qualities, and actions residing in [substances], such as existence (*sattā*), the nature of being a universal (*jātitva*), and the nature of being an action (*karmatva*) and so forth, we consider that since these too can possess identity (*tādātmya*) through a mediated succession, the contact is simply "identity with what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktatādātmya*). Or else, just as others resort to "inherence in what is inherent in the conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*) for the apprehension of the nature of color (*rūpatva*) and so forth, let there likewise be for us a third type of contact called "identity with the identity of that which is conjoined" (*saṃyuktatadātmatādātmya*). What loss is there?

Furthermore, it will be demonstrated later that the relationship between genus, quality, and action with their own substrata is indeed identity (*tādātmya*). Therefore, the sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) is either twofold or threefold. However, the followers of Tarka (the Naiyāyikas), substituting inherence (*samavāya*) for identity, describe the contact differently as being sixfold: conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), inherence in what is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), inherence (*samavāya*), inherence in what is inherent (*samavetasamavāya*), and the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).

In that regard, substances are apprehended through conjunction with the eyes and other sense organs. Qualities and so forth are apprehended through inherence in a substance that is conjoined with the eyes and other sense organs. Universals such as "quality-ness" (guṇatva) are apprehended through inherence in qualities and so forth that inhere in a substance conjoined [with the senses]. Furthermore, because sound is a quality of space (ākāśa), it is apprehended through inherence with the auditory organ, which consists of space. Universals such as "sound-ness" (śabdatva), however, are apprehended through inherence in sound, which inheres in the auditory organ.

However, since non-existence (abhāva) lacks both conjunction (saṃyoga) and inherence (samavāya)—the two properties possessed by positive entities—it is perceived through the contact consisting of the qualifier-qualified relationship (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva), as in the case of a surface and so forth that are conjoined [with a jar]. Likewise, because inherence itself is not a substance, it lacks conjunction; and if one were to postulate another inherence as its locus, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (anavasthā). Therefore, the contact is indeed the qualifier-qualified relationship alone.
Among these, the first triad [of contacts] differs only in name, whereas the other contacts, such as inherence and the rest, are without a basis. (Verse 8)

Since sound does not possess the quality of being an auditory object, the two types of contact known as *samavāya* (inherence) and *samavetasamavāya* (inherence in that which is inherent) are rendered impossible. Furthermore, because non-existence (*abhāva*) is not perceptible and inherence (*samavāya*) is as non-existent as a hare’s horn, the contact known as the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) must also be rejected. Moreover, the relation of qualifier and qualified cannot occur between an object conjoined with the eye and either non-existence or inherence.

In cases such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī puruṣaḥ*), the relationship between qualifier and qualified is always seen to be preceded by another [primary] relation; furthermore, since non-existence (*abhāva*) and inherence (*samavāya*) lack any other relation with their objects. However, the Prābhākaras maintain that sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) is threefold: conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), and inherence (*samavāya*). In their view, because [qualities like] "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) do not exist, inherence in what is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*) need not be accepted; likewise, because "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) does not exist, inherence in the inherent (*samavetasamavāya*) is also excluded.

Furthermore, since non-existence itself does not exist and since inherence lacks perceptibility, the relation of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva) cannot be accepted as a basis [for perception] either. That view has been refuted by the logicians themselves through the proof of [the existence of] generic properties such as "color-ness" (rūpatva). Therefore, the sense-object contact is indeed of the form previously described.

And that cognition produced by sense-object contact is of two kinds: non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*). Among these, the indistinct cognition that arises immediately after sense-object contact—which apprehends only the essential nature of a substance and so forth, and is devoid of the association with words—is called "non-conceptual" because of the absence of the construction of qualifications.

However, that cognition which follows immediately thereafter—accompanied by the recollection of words and having as its object a thing qualified by genus (*jāti*) and other attributes, such as "this jar is red" or "this is a cow"—is conceptual (*savikalpaka*). Regarding this, the Grammarians (*Śābdikas*) assert that there is no indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*). As they have said: "There is no cognition in the world that is not accompanied by words. This is incorrect; for if there were no prior perception of the object, it would follow that there is no cause for the recollection of words.

The Buddhists, however, relying solely on non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), assert that conceptual perception (*savikalpaka*) possesses neither the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) nor the nature of perception itself. This too is untenable; for if one were to deny that which is established in the world as being perceptual, it would contradict worldly consensus. As it has been said:
"He who denies that the moon is denotable by the word 'moon' would likewise be the one to obstruct the perceptual nature of conceptual cognition."

Thus it is said. Furthermore, since the observation of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) occurs immediately after conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency, is difficult to deny. If it is argued: "Its capacity for causal efficiency is merely adventitious (*daivāgata*), arising from the absence of extreme distance from the object; it is not intrinsic. In reality, this conceptual cognition is false, because its objects—such as universals (*sāmānya*) and the like—are non-entities (*avastu*)," We reply: Not so.

Otherwise, it would follow that even conceptual inference (*anumāna-vikalpa*) lacks validity, and furthermore, because the reality of universals (*sāmānya*) and other categories will be established later. Therefore, determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Now, one might object: "Even so, how can this be designated by the term 'perception' (*pratyakṣa*), given that it lacks direct sensory origin (*akṣajatva*) due to the intervention of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*)? If that which is produced through a causal chain from the senses were considered perception, then it would follow that inference and the like are also perception. This is not so.

If one accepts both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)—as in the case of words like *paṅkaja* (mud-born)—then the term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) would not apply to inference and the other means of knowledge. To this, the Guru says: "There is no conventional usage for words like *paṅkaja*; its application to the lotus is established through the power of its constituent parts alone. As for its non-application to white water-lilies and the like, that will simply result from the fact that it is not used for them. This is incorrect.

When considering what constitutes the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the application of the word *paṅkaja* (lotus) to a lotus, since mere etymological derivation (*yoga*) is found to deviate—being present even in the case of water-lilies (*kumuda*) and so forth—it must be postulated that conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is also part of the causal complex. Furthermore, since the perceived etymological meaning cannot be abandoned, both are established. Therefore, it is proven that by virtue of the combined power of etymology and convention (*yogarūḍhi*), only non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*) [perceptions] are denoted by the term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), and not inference (*anumāna*) and the rest, even though they depend on the senses.

Furthermore, conceptualization (*savikalpaka*) occurs in five ways, through [the association of an object] with substance, genus, quality, action, and name—such as: "This is a bamboo," "This is a cowherd," "This is dark-complexioned," "This is singing," and "This is Govinda. Some maintain that recognition-perception (*pratyabhijñā-pratyakṣa*) is a sixth type of conceptualization; however, that is not correct, because it is included within conceptualization by name. For when a previously experienced form is recalled by means of a name, the conceptualization of an object as being qualified by that form is called "conceptualization by name" (*nāma-kalpanā*).

Therefore, the meaning of the phrase "this is Govinda" is this: "he who was previously apprehended by us as being denotable by the word 'Govinda' is indeed this very person. However, when the denotability by words is disregarded and the sole intent is the comprehension of the identity between the prior and subsequent forms, then the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) "that very same one is this" becomes manifest. And that recognition is produced as a single cognition by means of the sense organ conjoined with mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). By that [recognition], two appearances are produced: "I" and "this."

In this context, the phrase "that" refers to the power to produce a manifestation caused by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), while "this" refers to the power to produce a manifestation caused by the sense organ. Enough of this digression. Here, in the case of perceptual cognitions, the status of being the instrument (*karaṇa*) belongs either to the sense organ or to the cognition resulting from its contact [with the object], depending on the speaker's intention. Therefore, it is established that perception is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) born from the contact of the sense organs. But the Teacher says: "Perception is immediate apprehension; it consists of a triad, namely the object, the knower, and the act of knowing."

In this regard, what is this so-called "immediacy" (*sākṣāttva*)? Is it not the case that immediacy is the cognition of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*), since through the sense-organ (*akṣa*) there is an appearance in its very own form? If it is argued that [cognition] derived from a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth is non-immediate because fire and the like appear only as related to something else, then conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) would also be non-immediate, since it appears as related to other things such as names (*nāman*) and so on.

Now, if it is argued that even when the form of another related object appears therein, there is also a cognition of its own form (*svarūpa*), then in the case of inference and so forth as well, there would be directness (*sākṣāttva*) because of that same state. Furthermore, we shall refute the claim that the self (*ātman*) and its own nature (*svātman*) are perceptible in all cognitions; let this matter rest for now. The Buddhists define perception (*pratyakṣa*) as "free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*)."

By the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*), conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) are excluded; by the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*), those cognitions such as the perception of a mass of hair—which, though non-conceptual, are considered erroneous—are excluded. However, even that [definition] is underinclusive (*avyāpta*), because it fails to establish the status of determinate perception (*savikalpaka*) as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, the logicians have stated that since the knowledge of yogins and the knowledge of Īśvara regarding objects such as the past and the future are immediate (*aparokṣa*) even in the absence of being produced by sense-object contact, perception (*pratyakṣa*) must be defined as "that which pervades immediate valid cognition" (*aparokṣapramāvyāpta*) in order to include them. That too is incorrect; for since perception is necessarily restricted to the apprehension of what is presently existing (*vidyamānopalambhatva*), it is impossible for the past and so forth to be perceptible. Therefore, the definition of perception stated by us is the correct one.
[Now follows: Substances other than the senses, and their respective classes...
And it will be stated that qualities and actions are generally perceptible. || 9 ||
Thus ends the examination of perception in the section on the means of valid cognition within the *Mānameyodaya*. Now follows the examination of inference.

Inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition of an object not present to the senses (*asannikṛṣṭārtha*) based on the perception of its pervader (*vyāpaka*). For example, from the perception of the presence of smoke on a mountain, there arises the cognition of the presence of fire. What constitutes the state of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*) in this case? It is said: that which does not exist outside of another is pervaded by that [other]. Smoke, moreover, does not exist elsewhere than where fire is; thus, smoke possesses the state of being pervaded. Fire, however, exists even elsewhere than where smoke is—such as in the state of glowing embers—and therefore it possesses only the state of being the pervader (*vyāpakatva*).

Thus, because there is no mutual pervasion (*vyāpti*) between fire and smoke, this is an instance of "unequal pervasion" (*viṣamavyāpti*). However, in some cases there is also "equal pervasion" (*samavyāpti*), as for example, between the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*). In that case, indeed, all things that are produced possess impermanence, and all things that are impermanent also possess the state of being produced; thus, it is indeed equal pervasion. What, then, is this pervasion? It is said: pervasion is an essential relationship (*svābhāvika-sambandha*). And its essential nature consists in the absence of any limiting condition (*upādhi*).

An *upādhi* (limiting condition) is defined as another reason that directly necessitates the probandum (*sādhya*). For when such a condition exists, the proposed reason—though it may occasionally obtain a connection with the probandum while possessing that condition—becomes non-probative by itself. An example is the argument of the non-Vedic Sāṅkhyas: "The killing of the sacrificial animal (*agnīṣomīya-hiṃsā*) is unrighteous (*adharma*), because it is a form of killing, like external killing. In this case, "being prohibited" (*niṣiddhatva*) is the *upādhi*. For that alone is the direct necessitant of unrighteousness.

Furthermore, the unrighteousness (*adharma*) of external acts of violence is established solely by virtue of their being prohibited; thus, in the case of ritual violence (*ṛtuhiṃsā*), since there is an absence of prohibition, its unrighteousness cannot be established merely by the fact of its being violence. The definition of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is: that which, while not pervading the probans (*sādhana*), is co-extensive with the probandum (*sādhya*). Indeed, "being prohibited" does not exist everywhere in the locus of the probans, namely "violence," because there is an absence of prohibition in the case of ritual violence.

Furthermore, there is a co-extensive pervasion (*samavyāpti*) between being prohibited and being unrighteousness (*adharman*), because all prohibited things are unrighteous, and all unrighteous things are prohibited. The three qualifiers [in the definition] are intended so that "possessing that causal complex" (*tatsāmagrīkatva*), "being a kitchen" (*mahānasatva*), and "being other than a mountain" (*parvatānyatva*) do not become adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) in the inference of fire.

In this context, if it were stated merely that "an *upādhi* is that which is co-extensive with the probandum (*sādhya*)," then, when fire-possessingness is being proved by means of smoke-possessingness, the possession of the causal complex for fire (*agnisāmagrīkatva*) would constitute an *upādhi*. For that [complex] indeed possesses co-extensiveness with fire; therefore, in order to exclude that, it is stated that [the *upādhi*] must be "non-pervasive of the probans" (*sādhanāvyāpaka*). Indeed, the causal complex for fire is necessarily pervasive of the smoke that serves as the probans, because wherever smoke exists, the causal complex for fire is invariably present.

If, however, one were to say merely that [the upādhi] does not pervade the probans (*sādhanāvyāpaka*), then in that very case, "being a kitchen" (*mahānasatva*) would become an *upādhi*. For when smoke is present, "being a kitchen" does not exist everywhere; thus, because it possesses the property of not pervading the probans, [it would falsely qualify as an *upādhi*]. Therefore, to exclude that possibility, one must rely on the property of "pervading the probandum" (*sādhyavyāpakatva*). Indeed, "being a kitchen" does not pervade fire, because even though fire exists in places such as monasteries (*maṭha*), "being a kitchen" is absent there.

Now, if it were stated merely that "an *upādhi* is that which, while not pervading the probans (*sādhana*), pervades the probandum (*sādhya*)," then even "being other than the mountain" (*parvatetaratva*) would be an *upādhi*. This is because smoke is observed on the mountain even in the absence of being other than the mountain, and thus it does not pervade the probans; yet, since all things previously determined to possess fire are also "other than the mountain," it exists as something that pervades the probandum. Therefore, the word "equal" (*sama*) is used to exclude that [case].

For there is no co-extensive concomitance (*samavyāpti*) between that [smoke] and fire, because not all things other than the mountain possess fire. Alternatively, the function of the qualification must be shown elsewhere: if an *upādhi* were necessarily co-extensive with the probandum (*sādhyasamavyāpta*), then in the argument "Sound is non-eternal, because it is produced, like a pot," "having an agent" (*sakartṛkatva*) would be an *upādhi*, since there exists a co-extensive concomitance between non-eternality and having an agent. Therefore, to exclude that, it was stated [in the definition] that it must be "non-pervasive of the probans" (*sādhanāvyāpaka*).

For "having an agent" is a pervader even of "being produced," which is intended as the probans; thus, because it is a pervader of the probans, it is not a valid *upādhi*. If, however, only that which does not pervade the probans were considered a valid *upādhi*, then why could "possessing parts" (*sāvayavatva*) or "being a jar" (*ghaṭatva*) not be an *upādhi* in that very same case? For these do not exist in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, which are indeed produced; thus, since they lack the property of being a non-pervader of the probans, the property of being a pervader of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) must also be required.

This is because properties such as "having parts" (*sāvayavatva*) and "being a jar" (*ghaṭatva*) do not possess pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) over "impermanence" (*anityatva*) in the case of qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and so forth. Nevertheless, since "otherness from sound" (*śabdetaratva*) does possess pervasion over impermanence, it would constitute a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); therefore, the word "equal" (*sama*) is used to exclude that. However, it should be understood that this inference is intended solely to demonstrate the pervasion (*vyāpti*), and is not intended to establish one's own final tenet (*svasiddhānta*).

[Objection: "But if fire were present even in the absence of 'otherness from the mountain,' this fault would arise; since such a *tarka* (reductio) is impossible, 'otherness from the mountain' does not possess pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) over fire. [Reply: True. Nevertheless, because that [otherness] is understood as a pervader, the word "equal" (*sama*) was employed by [the masters] such as Cidānanda and others for the sake of its effortless exclusion.
For only those things possessing equal pervasion (*samavyāpti*) are invariably considered *upādhis*.
Thus, the word "equal" is for the sake of clarity and is not a fault. (10)

Furthermore, when the pervasion of this limiting condition (*upādhi*) by the probandum (*sādhya*) and so forth is not certain, it is a "suspected" limiting condition (*śaṅkitopādhi*). For example, when it is to be proven that the eighth child of Maitrī’s son is dark-complexioned on the basis of being her son, the transformation of food such as vegetables is the limiting condition. While it is established that this [transformation] is absent in the case of the eighth son, its non-pervasion of the probans (*sādhana*) would indeed exist; yet, since that very absence is suspected even there, the non-pervasion of the probans remains uncertain. Therefore, this is a suspected limiting condition.

And sometimes it is the specific property of the probans (*sādhana*) itself that serves as the motivator [for exclusion]. For example, in the case [of the argument]: "This twice-born man will be a knower of the Vedas, because he is twice-born," the state of being twice-born characterized by [the possession of] intellect and so forth is the limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Therefore, the summary [verse] is: "Those who desire a limiting condition should seek a property that does not reach the locus of the subject (*pakṣa*), but which pervades all similar instances (*sapakṣa*). (11)

Thus, since this kind of limiting condition (upādhi) does not exist in relation to its connection with fire, this connection is indeed inherent (svābhāvika). If it is asked, "How, then, is that inherent connection apprehended? it is said in reply:

First, having repeatedly observed the connection between smoke and fire in the kitchen and other such places, and having successively suspected that "kitchen-ness," "house-ness," "village-ness," and so forth, might be limiting conditions (upādhi), one rejects them by observing their deviation. Having carefully examined other potential limiting conditions as well, one eliminates them through non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible. Then, by means of the sense organ aided by the mental impressions produced by the repeated observation and the grasping of the absence of limiting conditions, one determines: "This very same uniform, inherent connection between smoke and fire is indeed [the case]."

The Prābhākaras, however, maintain that the relation of smoke with fire is understood from a single observation alone; thus, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed cognizable through a single observation. They argue that repeated observation is sought only for the purpose of dispelling the suspicion of a limiting condition (*upādhi*). This is incorrect. Pervasion is defined as the very relation that constitutes a factor of inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, it is only a relation characterized by the absence of a limiting condition that serves as a factor of inference, not merely the relation between smoke and fire.

Furthermore, it has been stated by them that the determination of the absence of limiting conditions (*nirupādhikatva*) is indeed accomplished through repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*). Therefore, pervasion (*vyāpti*), which consists of a relation free from limiting conditions, is to be understood solely through repeated observation. [Objection: But the determination of the absence of limiting conditions cannot be achieved by mere repeated observation alone, since that [repeated observation] also exists in the case of "being the son of Maitrī" and "darkness of complexion. [Reply: True.

For this very reason, Citānanda says: "It is not only through repeated observation that such a certainty is established; rather, reasoning (*tarka*) which is conducive to the arising of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is also an auxiliary factor therein. But what is reasoning? It is said: Reasoning is the statement of a defect in the case of an alternative possibility, for the purpose of refuting the suspicion that an object being established by a means of valid cognition might otherwise be. For this very reason, logicians (*tārkika*) say that reasoning is the "reductio ad absurdum" (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*). And this alone is called the "sublating factor" (*bādhaka*) in the opposing position.

For example: "If there were no fire here, then there would be no smoke," and so forth. This *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) has five constituent parts, as they say: "Pervasion (*vyāpti*), non-frustration of the *tarka*, the conclusion (*avasāna*), [the undesirable consequence] in the contrary case (*viparyaya*)," and so on.

"The five limbs of *tarka* consist in [the undesirable], the non-conducive, and so forth. Here, having superposed the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*), such as the absence of fire, one employs *tarka* to entail an undesirable consequence, such as the absence of smoke, by means of that [superposed state] acting as the mark (*liṅga*). In that context, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the superimposed mark—which is brought about through mental imposition (*āhārya*)—must be accepted with respect to the consequence to be entailed. Likewise, there must be no contradiction by counter-*tarkas* (*pratitarka*), and there must be a finality in the reversal of the consequence to be entailed; that is, "if it were thus, it would be so," but "it is not thus."

It is well known that the consequence to be drawn must be undesirable, meaning it is unfavorable and does not establish the opposite position. Furthermore, if there is a deficiency in its constituent parts, it becomes a fallacious reasoning (*tarkābhāsa*). For example, in the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*), one might say: "If it were not possessed of fire, then it would also not be a mountain."

Regarding obstruction by a counter-reasoning (*tarka-pratihati*), for example: when one employs the reasoning, "If this [cloud] were not possessed of rain, it would not be dense," there is an obstruction by the counter-reasoning, "If this were possessed of rain, then it would not be accompanied by a gale. Regarding the absence of a conclusion in the contrapositive form (*viparyaya-paryavasānābhāva*), for example: in the argument presented to a Mīmāṃsaka, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced," the reasoning is, "If it were not impermanent, then it would not be produced either."

In this regard, it cannot be concluded that "this [word] is produced," because for the Mīmāṃsaka position, sound lacks the quality of being produced. Its "desirability" (iṣṭatva) also lies precisely here, since the absence of being produced is accepted by him. Regarding its "favorability" (anukūlatva), as in the case of the argument, "The action [of the sun] is inferable because it is an action, like the action of the sun"—here the reasoning is that otherwise, action itself would not be established. And that [reasoning] is favorable even to those who maintain [the reality of] perception.

For it could also be argued by them that, having established [the means of knowledge] as being perception, otherwise there would be no sequence at all. Furthermore, defects such as self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) and others are included within *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum), because they consist in the occurrence of an undesirable consequence.
The defect of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) is when something is established by itself.
When one thing is established by this, and another by that, it becomes mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). (Verse 12)
By this [reasoning], one [cognition] arises from that, and from that another; thus there is a circle.
Furthermore, the apprehension of one after another, without touching the past [moment], is an infinite regress.

Both complexity (*gaurava*) and simplicity (*lāghava*) are universal criteria of reasoning (*tarka*). Complexity consists in an excess of assumptions, whereas simplicity is the minimization of assumptions. (14)
The nature of a logical consequence (prasaṅga) belongs only to that which is cumbersome (gaurava);
whereas the status of being a consequence belongs to parsimony (lāghava) by way of praising its merits in the probandum (sādhya). 15.

Where there is a favorable *tarka*—whether it be a defect [pointed out] by restating the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), or even a quality [established] in the probandum—it is conducive to the proof of the probandum because it assists in its establishment. (16)

"Reproaching the very thing to be proven (sādhya) by means of an undesirable consequence is *tarka*; it would be counterproductive because it obstructs the establishment of what is to be proven. (17) Furthermore, this *tarka*, by dispelling doubts regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) either at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) or at the moment the inference arises, purifies the pervasion and thus becomes an auxiliary to the inference. [Objection: But surely, even by this very *tarka*—"If there were no fire, then there would be no smoke"—the doubt regarding deviation is not removed, because the doubt remains that "even in the absence of fire, why might smoke not exist? [Reply: True.

For this very reason, the logicians (*tārkika*) maintain that one must proceed by the path of reasoning (*tarka*) until doubt is completely eliminated. In this context, when the reasoning is applied—"If smoke were to exist even in the absence of fire, then it would have to be admitted that an effect is produced even without a cause"—the doubt, "Why should that [absence of fire] not also be possible? does not sprout in the minds of those who know the world. [Objection: Even so, the doubt as to why fire is determined to be the cause of smoke does not depart. [Reply: Not so.

If fire were not the cause, then—in the absence of any other perceived cause—it would follow by logical necessity (*tarka*) that smoke is entirely causeless; since this [conclusion] prevails over all [other possibilities], when such a *tarka* has eliminated every doubt of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), even the talk of suspecting another limiting condition (*upādhi*) is utterly dispelled. Consequently, the Cārvāka’s wicked doctrine—that the suspicion of an imperceptible limiting condition is altogether impossible to ward off—is also driven out. Alternatively, it is clearly shown that the very suspicion of a limiting condition is expelled: "Is the limiting condition one capable of being apprehended by a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), or is it incapable of such? (18)
"If he is unfit, one should not suspect him; if he is fit, why is he not seen?

If he is to be known through inference and the like, why are the logical marks (liṅga) and so forth not seen? (19), and so on. Consequently, in all inferences, this [process] continues until the obstruction of doubt is removed.
The web of reasoning should be employed; indeed, this that has been stated is very brief. || 20 ||
For all means of valid cognition, such as perception and verbal testimony, do not function without reasoning; let this first be observed in the case of perception. (21)

The perception "this is a jar" indeed has as its object the whole (avayavin), being supported by reasoning that excludes the possibility of its having atoms—as taught by the Sugata—as its objective domain. The reasoning is this: if it had atoms as its objective domain, then there would be no appearance of it as a single unit or as something large. Similarly, the perception "this is a cow," if it were to have an entirely distinct objective domain [from the individual], would result in the cognition "in this, there is cowness"; thus, being supported by such reasoning, it apprehends even non-difference, and so forth.

We say the same regarding verbal testimony (*śābda*). First of all, if the injunction for Vedic study were to have heaven as its fruit, then—since a visible purpose is possible—it would involve the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) by assuming an invisible result; thus, supported by reasoning (*tarka*), it is understood to have the knowledge of meaning as its fruit. Furthermore, the counter-reasoning that "if it had the knowledge of meaning as its fruit, the injunction would be purposeless" must be refuted in each respective case. Likewise, there is the traditional law (*smṛti*): "That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and the secret portions (*rahasya*), him they call an *ācārya*."

If this were a rule for the procedure of teaching (*adhyāpanavidhi*), then it would not form a single syntactical unit with the portion, "But that twice-born man they call an *ācārya*"; thus, by means of such reasoning (*tarka*), it is determined that this Smṛti has the definition of an *ācārya* as its primary purpose. Similarly, in the case of the injunction, "One should place the smeared pebbles," if the smearing were not done with ghee, then the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), "Ghee is indeed splendor," would be contradicted; therefore, by means of such reasoning, the purpose of smearing with ghee is established. In this way, in all cases, the appearance of false meanings is set aside through various forms of reasoning.
The entire Mīmāṃsā system, appearing in the form of a tree, establishes the meaning of sentences.
And it has been said by Manu:
"He who investigates the instruction on dharma given by the ṛṣis through reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures— he, and no other, knows dharma."
In this way, one should infer that in each respective case, tarka is required even for analogy (upamāna), presumption (arthāpatti), and non-existence (abhāva).
Therefore, tarka stands as a supportive factor for all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Its support consists in the severing of the suspicion regarding the opposite of what is to be proven (sādhya). (23)
The object whose true nature is not yet known is considered the subject in doubt;
the reason is the superimposed mark (liṅga); and the result is the determination of the true nature of the object. (24)
Thus, when one describes things otherwise than they are for the sake of establishing reality, there proceeds a succession of fallacious superimpositions and their proofs. (25)

In that regard, there may even be some confusion regarding the status of a tenet when it involves superimposition or denial; for if the Veda is dependent upon God, then God himself cannot be established [as independent]. (26)
When this is said, one might think that the non-existence of God is the established tenet;
yet, due to the superimposition of what is impossible, dissatisfaction may arise in some cases. (27)
If the atom were thus without a fixed limit to its reduction, then,
because it would be composed of infinite constituent parts, there would be no difference between Mount Meru and a mustard seed.
So that the statement "it may have an equal magnitude" and so forth may be applicable, this reasoning (tarka) is employed for the establishment of that means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). (29)
One who clearly discerns that "this is something else that has been stated" is not deluded at all;
therefore, this method of reasoning, even though it has arrived as a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum), [is valid]. (30)

"I have set forth in detail [the argument] that [the relationship] is an ultimate benefactor" (v. 301). Thus, in this way, the relation free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhika-sambandha*) is determined by repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) aided by reasoning (*tarka*). Through repeated observation, the elimination of perceptible limiting conditions is possible.

"But the suspicion of an invisible limiting condition (*upādhi*) is refuted by those very [means]. This is the distinction. Therefore, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established. The Buddhists, however, say that the establishment of pervasion occurs only through identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*). For example: there is identity in the pervasion of "being a *śiṃśapā* tree" by "being a tree," and there is causality in the pervasion of "smoke" by "fire. That is not so; because both [identity and causality] are absent in the pervasion of the rising of the Kṛttikā star by the proximity of Rohiṇī. Therefore, the establishment of pervasion occurs only from the ascertainment of the absence of a limiting condition. Pervasion is necessity, connection, non-deviation, and likewise inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*).
Furthermore, the pervaded (vyāpya) is that which is to be determined; it is the indicator (gamaka), the mark (liṅga), the means of proof (sādhana), and the reason (hetu). ||32||
Thus, these are the synonyms for both; however, his [the yogin’s] vision is threefold. //33//

At the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the first [moment] is the perception of smoke; the second is the perception of smoke by one who has gone to the vicinity of a mountain; and third is the subsequent reflection (*anusandhāna*) that "such smoke exists here" following the recollection of the pervasion. It is this perception of the pervaded (*vyāpyadarśana*) that is intended here, because the knowledge of fire arises immediately after it. But what is meant by the term "not proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭa*)? We say it means "unascertained. As it has been said: "By the word 'not proximate,' two things are here intended to be excluded..."

"...determination occurs either through that very form or through its opposite. For if fire and so forth have already been determined as existing, then a subsequent inference would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*); and if they were determined as non-existent, it would lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*) because it would be sublated. To exclude both of these possibilities, the term "not proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭa*) is used. Here, the Cārvākas argue: if a specific fire were the object of inference, the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) would not be established; for the concomitance exists only between the generality of fire and the generality of smoke.

If, however, the universal (*sāmānya*) were the object of inference, then because it has already been determined previously, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*). Consequently, even the term "not proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭa*) would be inappropriate. As it has been said:
"In this mire that destroys inference, the elephants of the disputants are submerged."

"In the case of particulars, there is no universal concomitance; in the case of universals, it would be a proof of what is already established. To this it is replied: First of all, the establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) does not occur between two universals alone. For if that were the case, the apprehension of pervasion would consist in the fact that "fire-ness" (*vahnitva*) is inherently connected with "smoke-ness" (*dhūmatva*). Consequently, due to its connection with the universal fire-ness, smoke-ness itself would be fire. Therefore, the pervasion between two universals is established only by means of particulars.

Furthermore, because those specific features vary in each instance, they cannot be determined as fixed; thus, the established position is that pervasion (*vyāpti*) pertains to two things characterized by non-fixed particulars. Consequently, smoke seen as existing on a mountain leads to the inference of fire on that mountain as being characterized by non-fixed particulars.

And here, although the universal fire (*agni-sāmānya*), unqualified by any specific [particularity], is grasped at the very time of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and that alone is the object of inference (*anumeya*), nevertheless, because at this moment the specific place and time—namely, "fire exists on the mountain"—are also being inferred, and because that [specificity] was not previously established, there is no possibility of the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhyatva*). The learned know that the two factors—the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—are the limbs of inference. Through the mode joined with pervasion, there is the cognition of the universal fire; while the property of the subject consists in the smoke’s residing upon the mountain. (34)

"By that [cognition], the connection of the mountain with fire is also understood. To this, the teacher says: "Since the fact that a place possessing smoke also possesses fire was already grasped at the time of apprehending the pervasion (vyāpti), it is now only the mountain's possession of smoke that is to be grasped as something new; its possession of fire, however, is understood as having been previously grasped. This is incorrect, for it has already been stated that the mountain's possession of smoke is indeed grasped only at this moment.

Therefore, for one who does not investigate how the apprehension of fire could have previously existed here without the apprehension of smoke, this is merely the delusion of the teacher. Thus, it is established that inference is knowledge of what is not in contact [with the senses]. And here, the nature of knowledge as inference has been stated precisely because it is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of inferential cognition (*anumiti*) in the form of manifestation (*prākaṭya*), according to the method explained by the authorities. Furthermore, since smoke and other such signs are the instruments of inferential cognition in the form of knowledge, they too certainly possess the status of inference.

That inference is of three kinds: positive-negative (*anvayavyatirekin*), purely positive (*kevalānvayin*), and purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*). For pervasion (*vyāpti*) is twofold: positive pervasion (*anvayavyāpti*) and negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*). Among these, the presence of the probandum (*sādhya*) when there is the presence of the probans (*sādhana*) is positive pervasion; the absence of the probans when there is the absence of the probandum is negative pervasion. Furthermore, in the case of negation, the relationship between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is the reverse of that in the positive case. For here, the absence of fire is the pervaded, and the absence of smoke is the pervader.
Because the state of fire is predominant, its absence becomes minor;
and because the state of smoke is minor, its absence is more extensive. (36)

Thus is the justification for the distinction [between the types of inference]. Among these, that which possesses both kinds of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the *anvaya-vyatirekin* (positive-negative). An example is the inference of fire from smoke and so forth. For in that case, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of smoke with fire is observed in places such as a kitchen; likewise, the absence of smoke in the absence of fire is observed in places such as a great lake. Therefore, it possesses the nature of being both positive and negative. On the other hand, that which possesses only positive pervasion is the *kevalānvayin* (purely positive). An example is: "Cognition is manifested by another cognition, because it is an entity, like a jar," and so forth.

For here, in the absence of being manifested by knowledge (*jñānaprakāśyatva*), the absence of being a real entity (*vastutva*) cannot be demonstrated anywhere, because all objects whatsoever are manifested by knowledge. Therefore, there is an absence of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*). That which possesses only negative concomitance is a *kevalavyatirekin* [inference]. For example: "All knowledge is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*) because it is knowledge; for that which lacks self-luminosity, knowledge-ness also does not exist, as in the case of a jar."

For here, since it is impossible to demonstrate anywhere that whatever possesses self-luminosity also possesses the nature of being a cognition, there is no positive concomitance (anvayavyāpti). This very reason, which is purely negative (kevalavyatirekin), is also called an *āvīta* reason. However, the followers of Kumārila generally do not accept such a negative inference;
instead, they consecrate a fifth means of valid cognition (*pramiti*) in its place. (37)
For that which is well-known in one place is established elsewhere by means of inference;
however, the property of self-luminosity is not established anywhere else. (38)
Therefore, in proving that [point], the subject (pakṣa) has an unestablished qualifier; and thus, let this defective subject, namely the negative-only (vyatirekī) inference, be rejected. (39)
Furthermore, the claim made by logicians that there is no fault when a favorable *tarka* exists—even if the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*)—is inconsistent. (40)
"For reasoning (tarka) is never capable of establishing a matter that is not already established [in some general sense].
Therefore, even when reasoning is employed, the fault of the unestablished nature of the predicate (aprasiddhatā-doṣa) is difficult to avoid.

(41) [Objection: But surely, by this means of knowledge—namely, "The state of being an object of cognition (vedyatva) does not exist at all in anything, because it is a property (dharma), just as the state of being a jar (ghaṭatva) does not exist in cloth and so forth"—the self-luminous nature (svayaṃprakāśatva), which consists in the absence of being an object of cognition, is established in a general way; and since it is then established specifically within the subject (pakṣa), the subject does not suffer from the fault of having an unestablished qualification (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva). As it has been said:

"Even when the qualifier is established through general inference (*sāmānyato'numāna*), tell me, how can this subject (*pakṣa*) be said to have an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*)? Or, let it be so. For this very reason, Citānanda [accepts] the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*).
He neither directly rejected nor did he directly accept. || 42 ||
Therefore, it is established that those who lack spiritual accomplishment and are prone to transgression must be restrained in every way; this much is settled. (43)
And here, regarding self-luminosity, there is no inference based on generality; for since it is a property such as "being a real entity," its absolute non-existence cannot occur anywhere. (44) Thus.

In this context, there are five characteristics of a reason (*hetu*) that possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekin*): (1) being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), (2) presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣe sattva*), (3) exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣād vyāvṛttatva*), (4) having a non-sublated object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), and (5) having no counter-balancing reason (*asatpratipakṣatva*). Among these, the "subject" (*pakṣa*) is a mountain or the like, wherein the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is sought to be known. The reason's being established in that [subject] is its "being a property of the subject. A "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) is a kitchen or the like, wherein the property to be proven is already ascertained. Its existing therein is its "presence in the similar instances. A "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*) is a great lake or the like, wherein the absence of the property to be proven is ascertained.

In that context, "not occurring therein" means exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). "The probandum being uncontradicted" means having an uncontradicted object. "The absence of a counter-reason" means being without a rival argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*). However, for a purely positive reason (*kevalānvayin*), there is no exclusion from the counter-example because of the non-existence of a counter-example; therefore, it possesses four characteristics. For a purely negative reason (*kevalavyatirekin*), there is no presence in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) because of the non-existence of a similar instance.

If, however, a reason were to reside in the subject alone even when a similar instance (sapakṣa) exists, it would indeed be the fallacious reason known as the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa). For example: "The earth is eternal, because it possesses odor. Here, although there exist similar instances such as space (ākāśa) which are eternal, the possession of odor resides in the earth alone. Therefore, logicians define a "purely negative" (kevalavyatirekin) reason as one that resides in the subject alone when no similar instance exists. As it is said: "That which is situated only in the subject may be established by a reason situated only in the subject; for the power to attract what resides elsewhere belongs only to that [reason] which is already present therein. (45)
Therefore, because it lacks presence in the similar class (sapakṣa), the purely negative inference (vyatirekī) possesses only four forms.
Thus, it is established that inference is twofold or threefold.

Furthermore, that [inference] is seen to be of two kinds: *dṛṣṭa* (perceived) and *sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa* (generally perceived). Among these, *dṛṣṭa* is held by those like me to have as its object a single perceived individual, such as the inference of Rohiṇī’s rising upon observing the rising of Kṛttikā. (463)
Thus, that which is inferred through the observation of a general pervasion is "inference based on what is generally observed" (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa), such as the inference of fire and the like. (47)

The logicians and others, however, say: "Inference concerning objects suitable for perception, such as fire, is *dṛṣṭa* (perceived); inference concerning supersensible objects, such as the eye, is *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* (seen through generality). This is incorrect. Since supersensible objects cannot be inferred, even the existence of the eyes and other senses is established only through *arthāpatti* (presumption). For instance—the word "because of pervasion" (*vyāpteḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence—it is an established principle that inference has pervasion (*vyāpti*) as its sole refuge. How, then, could it possibly deviate from the path shown by that pervasion? (483)
Therefore, in the cognition of pervasion (vyāpti), whatever kind of object is perceived, it must be inferred as being exactly like that, just as fire is hot and luminous. (493)
Furthermore, supersensible objects cannot possess a previously perceived form;
for visibility is observed in luminous bodies, and that is impossible in the case of the eye. (50)
For this very reason, we shall proclaim as a fault called "the sublation of the specific" (viśeṣabādhaka) in every case where there is a means of proof for something absolutely unobserved. (513)

"Therefore, the eyes and other [faculties] are established through the fact that the manifestation of form and so forth would otherwise be impossible; it is not held that there is inference regarding them [directly]. (523) They say that this inference is also twofold, by way of the distinction between inference for oneself (*svārtha*) and inference for others (*parārtha*). That in which one infers for oneself alone, having seen smoke and the like and having ascertained the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, is inference for oneself.
When, however, that very same object is understood through the words of another, then they call it "for the sake of others" (parārtha); such is the extent of the difference between these two.

In this regard, the logicians (tārkikas) maintain that the statement of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) consists of five members (*pañcāvayava*). These members are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). For instance: "This mountain possesses fire" (proposition); "because it possesses smoke" (reason); "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, just as a kitchen" (example); "and this [mountain] possesses smoke" (application); "therefore, it certainly possesses fire" (conclusion). Here, the statement of the subject (*pakṣa*) intended to inform another is the proposition: "The mountain possesses fire. The statement of the mark (*liṅga*) which makes known its status as a means of proof is the reason: "because it possesses smoke."

The statement of an example preceded by the demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the *udāharaṇa*, such as: "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, just like a kitchen. The application (*upanaya*) is the application of that which has its pervasion established to the subject (*pakṣa*), such as: "And this [mountain] possesses smoke. The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the subject along with the reason, such as: "Therefore, it possesses fire. Regarding this, we say:
Since the conclusion is already covered by the proposition (*pratijñā*), the application by the reason, and likewise the rest, who would undertake the proclamation of five members? (543)
Therefore, we maintain that the syllogism consists of three members, free from redundancy; it either ends with the example or begins with the example. (551)

The Buddhists, however, say: "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, as in a kitchen; and this [mountain] possesses smoke"—by stating only this much, it follows by implication that "therefore, it possesses fire. Thus, they claim there are only two members: the example (*udāharaṇa*) and the application (*upanaya*). That too is rejected because it entails the fault of having to supply an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) regarding the probandum (*sādhya*). Therefore: "Thus, due to redundancy and likewise due to the fault of supplying an ellipsis, we abandon the system of the Logicians and the Buddhists and remain with three members [of the syllogism]. (563)

In this regard, an example [of the syllogism] ending with the *udāharaṇa* (illustration) is as follows: "The mountain possesses fire, because it possesses smoke; whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, just like a kitchen. An example beginning with the *udāharaṇa* is as follows: "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, just like a kitchen; and this [mountain] possesses smoke; therefore, it possesses fire.
Now, the refutation of the thesis (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) will be stated by us in due order, as it ought to be known before the disputants. (Verse 573)

In this context, the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) is indeed the expression of the position (*pakṣa*) for the purpose of communicating it to another. And it has been stated that the position is that which is qualified by the property (*dharma*) sought to be known. Consequently, because [the property] is either determined as being of that nature, or determined as its opposite, or because it is unestablished elsewhere, that which is not the property sought to be known cannot qualify the position. Therefore, a position whose qualification is already established, whose qualification is sublated, or whose qualification is unestablished is merely a pseudo-position (*pakṣābhāsa*); and the statement that makes such a thing known is likewise merely a pseudo-thesis (*pratijñābhāsa*).

For example: "Fire is hot" is one where the qualifier is established (*siddhaviśeṣaṇa*). "Fire is not hot" is one where the qualifier is sublated (*bādhitaviśeṣaṇa*). "The earth and so forth have an omniscient creator" is one where the qualifier is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*), because the state of having an omniscient creator is not established in any instance, such as a jar. The internal subdivisions of "sublated qualifier" (*bādhitaviśeṣaṇatva*) should be understood according to the different types of subverting evidence (*bādhakapramāṇa*). Among these, the sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) in the case of "fire is not hot" has been stated previously.

When an inference is also clearly powerful, then there is sublation by inference (*anumāna-bādha*). For example: "The mind is not a sense-organ (*indriya*), because it is not composed of the elements (*abhūtātmaka*), like space (*dik*) and so forth. Here, since the mind is inferred as being a sense-organ, its status as a non-sense-organ is sublated by that very inference which perceives the mind as the subject (*dharmin*). In this way, one should observe that inferences which occur more rapidly act as sublaters in all cases.

Verbal sublation (*śābdabādha*) is, for example: "Sacrifices and the like are not means to attain heaven, because they are actions, like walking. Here, since verbal statements such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" communicate that sacrifices are means to attain heaven, their non-existence is sublated by verbal testimony. Or, for example: "Human bone is touchable, because it is a part of a living being, like a conch shell. In the case of "A cow is not similar to a gavaya, because it is a living being, like a human," there is sublation by comparison (*upamāna*).

In the case of "Devadatta is not outside because he is not seen there," there is sublation by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), since his being outside is established through presumptive reasoning. In the case of "Air possesses color because it is a substance, like earth," there is sublation by non-perception (*anupalambha*). There are also other defects of the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*):

for instance, if one says, "I am silent for as long as I live," there is sublation by one's own statement; and if one says, "The moon is not to be called *candra*," there is contradiction with common worldly usage. (Verse 583)

"By the very same [reason] by which the impermanence of sound and so forth was previously stated, if permanence were stated again, there would be a contradiction of the prior discourse. (59) Thus, the property that pervades the probandum is the logical reason (*hetu*). There are four fallacies (*tadābhāsa*) of it: the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). Among these, the unestablished is now described.
The cognition of the reason as being connected to the subject (pakṣa) is called "establishment" (siddhi); for the fulfillment of the reason is achieved by that alone. (603)

If even one part among these were absent—namely, the reason (*hetu*), the locus (*pakṣa*), the connection (*sambandha*), or the apprehension (*graha*)—the [proof] would be unestablished (*asiddhatā*). (613)

In that context, when the very nature of the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished, it is a "reason unestablished in its own nature" (*svarūpāsiddha*). For example, in the argument "The Buddha is free from delusion because he is omniscient," omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) is not established for us anywhere. This [type of fallacy] has two subdivisions: the "unestablished in its qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*) and the "unestablished in its qualificand" (*viśeṣyāsiddha*). The first is, for instance, "The Buddha is a teacher of the Dharma because, while being omniscient, he possesses a body"; the other, however, is "because, while possessing a body, he is omniscient. When there is an absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is "unestablished in its state of being pervaded" (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*).

For example: "Sacrificial violence is unrighteous because it is violence. Here, due to the presence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*). In the absence of the subject (*pakṣa*), [the reason]...

The *āśrayāsiddha* (unestablished locus) is, for example: "A sky-flower is fragrant, because it is a flower. The *sambandhāsiddha* (unestablished relation) occurs when there is no connection between the reason and the subject; for example: "Sound is impermanent, because it is visible. That which lacks a connection with even a portion of the subject is the *bhāgāsiddha* (partially unestablished). This same fallacy is sometimes called *vyāptyasiddha* (unestablished pervasion) due to the absence of pervasion over the entire subject; for example: "The Vedas are of human origin, because they consist of narratives."

When, however, there is no connection with the subject (*pakṣa*) for either the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or the qualified (*viśeṣya*), then there occurs the "unestablishedness of the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*) and the "unestablishedness of the qualified" (*viśeṣyāsiddhi*). For example: "The sky is impermanent, because it is a substance while being produced," and "because it is produced while being a substance. But where the qualifier is useless due to the absence of anything to be excluded, and thus incapable of a [logical] connection, that is the "unestablishedness of a useless qualifier" (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇāsiddha*). For example: "A pot is impermanent, because it is a product while being a substance."

Thus, when "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is the reason, [the argument] "because it possesses substantiality" (*dravyatvāt*) is a case of an unestablished reason due to a redundant qualification (*vyarthaviśeṣyāsiddha*). However, when a reason is not employed as being related to the subject (*pakṣa*), but rather as being related to another locus, it is then an unestablished reason due to a difference in locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*). For example: "The pot is impermanent because its quality (*guṇa*) is produced. Here, the state of being produced does not reside in the pot itself, but resides in its quality; therefore, it is an unestablished reason due to a difference in locus.

That [reason] for which there is no connection with the subject (*pakṣa*) due to the absence of exclusion from the subject is "unestablished through exclusion" (*vyatirekā-siddha*). For example: "The sky is non-eternal, because it possesses sky-ness (*gaganatva*). Here, there is no such thing as "sky-ness" distinct from the very nature of the sky itself. When these [reasons], such as essential nature (*svarūpa*), are unknown, they become "unestablished through ignorance" (*ajñānāsiddha*) or "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddha*). For example: "Devadatta will possess great wealth, because he possesses unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) which is the cause thereof."

In this case, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of such an unperceived [property], and thus it is "unestablished due to ignorance" (*ajñātatva*). Similarly, in the formulation "the mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke," the reason is unestablished due to ignorance of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), because the pervasion has not been demonstrated. In the same way, the "unestablished due to a doubtful qualification" (*sandigdhaviśeṣaṇāsiddha*) and others should also be inferred as varieties of unestablished reasons due to ignorance. Logicians, however, maintain that "unestablished in its own nature" (*svarūpāsiddhi*) is simply the absence of the reason's own nature in the subject (*pakṣa*), and thus they claim that what is "unestablished in its relation" (*sambandhāsiddha*) is actually a case of "unestablished in its own nature. That is incorrect.

The nature of omniscience itself does not exist anywhere at all; however, as for [the property] such as "being visible to the eye," there is no connection with the subject (*pakṣa*)—this is because they are perceived as distinct. These are varieties of the unestablished (*asiddha*); when they are unestablished for only one of the two disputants, they are called "unestablished for one or the other" (*anyatarāsiddha*). In that regard, when it is stated, "Buddha is free from delusion because he is omniscient," this is unestablished for us alone. Likewise, when it is unestablished for both, it should be understood as "unestablished for both" (*ubhayāsiddha*), as for example: "A rabbit is predatory because it has horns. Now, the contradictory (*viruddha*).

And that is designated as "the sublater" (*bādhaka*) in the *Vārttika*; for it sublates in two ways: by sublation of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and by sublation of the specific qualification (*viśeṣa*). (621)

Among these, that which is pervaded by the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*) is the "contradictory to the nature of the probandum" (*sādhyasvarūpaviruddha*). For example: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced. Here, since being produced is pervaded by non-eternality—the opposite of eternality—it contradicts eternality and thus serves as its sublater (*bādhaka*). That which is pervaded by a qualification opposite to the qualification of the probandum is the "contradictory to the qualification" (*viśeṣaviruddha*). For example: "The earth and so forth have an agent, because they are effects, like a pot."

In this case, the specific attribute of the probandum—the creator of the earth and so forth—is bodilessness (*aśarīritva*). Since in things such as jars, the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is observed to be pervaded by its opposite, the specific attribute of embodiedness (*śarīritva*), this [embodiedness] constitutes a sublation (*bādhaka*) of bodilessness.
