And when bodilessness is sublated, the status of having a creator is also sublated, since the specific attribute of embodiedness has been sublated by perception. (633)

"Having attained bodilessness, I shall remain"—one who makes such an effort [is refuted], for even the agency of that [agent] perishes when [the self] is sublated, being left without a substratum. Thus, because it contradicts the probandum, this is indeed a flaw for us. To those logicians who do not understand such a thing, I offer this salutation with joined palms.

The *savyabhicāra* (deviant) reason is the *anaikāntika* (inconclusive). That is to say, it is that which exists even in the *vipakṣa* (the dissimilar class). It is also called *sādhāraṇa* (common). For example: "Sound is non-eternal, because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*). Here, since knowability exists even in eternal things, the reason is inconclusive. However, where the existence [of the reason] in the *vipakṣa* is doubtful, that is the *sandigdhānaikāntika* (doubtfully inconclusive).

For example, in the argument "entities are momentary because they exist," since there is no sublation (*bādhā*) of existence even if [the entities] were non-momentary, the presence of the reason in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) becomes suspected. When a similar class (*sapakṣa*) exists, that which occurs in the subject (*pakṣa*) alone is the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason. For example: "The earth is eternal because it possesses odor. However, some say that even the uncommon reason is indeed "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).

Just as the property of being knowable (*prameyatva*) is inconstant because it occurs even in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), so too the property of possessing odor (*gandhavattva*) is inconstant because it occurs in all similar examples (*sapakṣa*), having overstepped its own proper domain, the counter-example, of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). True; however, it is only the positive concomitance that has overstepped its own proper domain. Your proposed sequence is laborious and is known as "inconstancy" (*vyabhicāra*). (661) Therefore, it is the "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) reason alone that is declared to be inconstant; the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) is declared to be a distinct fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). (673)

Alternatively, even according to the path you have stated, since that [reason] also suffers from deviation, let it simply be considered inconclusive; there is no loss for us whatsoever. Therefore, fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are established as being either threefold or fourfold; logicians say they are fivefold, while others say sixfold—that is inconsistent. (683, 691)

Logicians maintain that there are five types [of fallacious reasons], distinguished as: the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), the equal-to-the-issue (*prakaraṇasama*), and the mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). Some say there is a sixth, the non-probative (*aprayojaka*); Bhāsarvajña, however, holds that the sixth is simply the undetermined (*anadhyavasita*). Among these, a reason that possesses a counter-reason is called *prakaraṇasama* or *satpratipakṣa*. For example: "Air is not perceptible because it lacks color, like the mind"; and "Air is perceptible because it possesses touch, like a jar."

This [fallacy] must be subsumed within those already mentioned. For instance: first, two contradictory reasons of equal strength cannot possibly exist; for if that were the case, it would follow that a single entity possesses two contradictory forms simultaneously, each established by the force of its respective inference. When there is a conflict between a strong and a weak reason, the weak one—its object having been usurped by the strong—is nothing other than what is termed a "defect of the subject" (*pakṣadoṣa*) due to its being characterized as sublated (*bādhita*). What, then, is the point of speaking of it as a separate fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*)?

[Objection: "But surely, at the time when no distinction between the two reasons is perceived, there is the possibility of their having equal strength based on mere presumption; therefore, there is 'balancing the reason' (*prakaraṇasama*) at that moment. [Reply: Not so. Even then, let there simply be the state of doubt regarding the qualification being sublated (*bādhitaviśeṣaṇatva*); one need not search for a separate category of fallacy. Otherwise, even cases such as the "doubtful unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddha*) would have to be considered distinct categories. Alternatively, the definition of the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) reason is adopted as: "that which is a cause of doubt."

Doubt arises from common characteristics (*sādhāraṇadharma*), uncommon characteristics (*asādhāraṇadharma*), and conflicting testimony (*vipratipatti*). For example: from the common characteristic of height, one doubts whether it is a post or a person; from the uncommon characteristic of possessing odor, one doubts whether earth is eternal or non-eternal; and from the conflicting testimony of disputants, one doubts whether sound is eternal or non-eternal. Among these, doubt caused by conflicting testimony occurs when a counter-argument is employed; therefore, it should be subsumed under the "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) fallacy, which is itself a type of the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) reason.

And when a counter-proof is established against this very argument by means of a single reason, there arises a sub-classification known as *viruddhāvyabhicārī* (the non-erroneous contradictory). For example: "The earth and so forth have an agent because they are effects, like a pot," versus "The earth and so forth do not have God as their agent because they are effects, like a pot. Here, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is non-deviant (*avyabhicarita*) with respect to both having an agent—as seen in pots and the like—and the absence of having God as the agent.

Furthermore, the absence of God’s authorship is directly contradictory to those who seek to prove God by means of the property of having an agent; thus, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is characterized as "non-deviant contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicāritva*).

Thus, when the proof is contradicted by the very same thesis, reason, and example propounded by the opponent, we maintain that there is "non-deviation from the contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicāritā). (70) The Teachers have sometimes spoken of non-deviation from the contradictory in the case of all counter-arguments (satpratipakṣa), and not only in this specific instance alone. (71) However, by Citānanda, this very [instance] is clearly stated in that manner. Whether it be so or otherwise, let it be; for us, there is no other fallacy (ābhāsa) here. (72)

Thus it is established that the refutation known as *sapratisādhanatva* (the state of having a counter-argument) is included within either the "sublated" (*bādhita*) or the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) fallacies. However, Bhāsarvajña, having stated that a reason possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) is *prakaraṇasama* even when it establishes both one's own position and the opponent's position, provides a single example of this which is difficult to find: for instance, "Sound is non-eternal, because it is one of the two—either the subject or the similar instance—just like the similar instance."

For here one could indeed say: "Sound is eternal, because it is one or the other of the two—either the subject (pakṣa) or the similar instance (sapakṣa). But this is incorrect. In this context, when "impermanence" is the property to be proven (sādhya), the meaning of "because it is one or the other of the subject and the similar instance" is "because it is one or the other of sound and a jar. However, when "eternality" is the property to be proven, the meaning is "because it is one or the other of sound and space. Therefore, how can it be said that the same single reason (hetu) is identical in both cases?

In this case, there exists only a similarity of words, while the actual meaning differs. Therefore, how could there be a pervasion (vyāpti) by two contradictory properties? [73] How then do you speak of the "non-erroneous contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārin)? It is true that in that case, the opposite of the probandum (sādhyaviparyaya) is not directly established. [74] For those who assert that [the world] has an agent, the agency of Īśvara is desired; it is precisely that which is being refuted by us here, and not a contradiction by implication. [75]

"But you, by attempting today to prove through a single [reason] that which is directly contradictory—namely, impermanence and permanence—will surely fall into ridicule. (763) As for that fallacy of the reason called *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed), which is synonymous with "having a sublated object," such as the example "fire is not hot because it is not a substance," this too is simply a fallacy of the thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*) known as "having a sublated qualification.
[Objection: But we do not even admit the existence of faults in the thesis; for the faults of the thesis and the example are included within the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). (77)

In that regard, concerning the case where the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is unestablished: "The subject (*pakṣa*), indeed, is the locus of the reason, and it does not possess a property that is [already] ascertained; therefore, it possesses the status of being a subject (*pakṣatva*). Consequently, that is simply the 'unestablished locus' (*āśrayāsiddhi*). (781) "If, in the same way, there were a fault consisting of an 'unestablished qualification,' even then, because the status of being a subject is lost, let it be called 'unestablished locus. (79) Furthermore, what is the point of stating faults of the subject (*pakṣadoṣa*) now?

The faults of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*), which will be discussed later, are indeed already included within the faults of the reason (*hetudoṣa*); for there is no fault other than the fault of the reason. Thus, since all faults enter into the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), how could that [reason] whose qualification has been sublated remain without support? (81) 813)
Therefore, like other fallacies, that which has a sublated qualification must also be stated as a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) itself. To this, we reply:

Regarding the confusion of appearances, it is indeed beyond dispute among all disputants that a fault manifesting before one's eyes must first be pointed out. Therefore, if some fault appears in the statement of the thesis (*pakṣa*), it should be declared as a fault of the thesis itself; why would you not accept this logic? (823–83) For even by us, the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) was stated in reliance solely upon the defectiveness of the thesis, as in the case of [the argument] where the qualifier is unestablished (*asiddhaviśeṣaṇa*). What will there be for you that manifests before you [in that case]? (843) In this way, the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the sublated nature of the probandum (*bādhitasādhyatā*) manifest precisely in the statement of the thesis; thus, their status as defects of the thesis is appropriate. (85)

Thus, the faults of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*) and those yet to be mentioned have been established, based on the determination that whichever fault manifests in a particular case belongs to that very case alone. [Verse 86] The Sage Akṣapāda did not mention faults of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) and so forth in the past; let us not abandon logic, O logicians, deluded as we are by devotion to him! [Verse 87] Therefore, since a thesis with a sublated qualification (*bādhitaviśeṣaṇa*) is merely a fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*), a fifth type of fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) should not be admitted.

Furthermore, those who maintain that there is a distinct fallacy of the reason called "non-probative" (*aprayojaka*)—on the grounds that a reason lacks probative force in the absence of a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*)—they too consider this to be merely a case of "unestablished pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*). For in all inferences, one must establish the presence of an unconditioned relation (*nirupādhikatva*) by removing the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) through a favorable argument. Therefore, in its absence, because the unconditioned connection cannot be ascertained, there is simply no establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

This very reason, whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished because it possesses a limiting condition (*upādhi*), is designated as "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddha*), "non-conclusive" (*aprayojaka*), "dependent on a pervasion propounded by another," and "of doubtful pervasion" (*sandigdhavyāptika*); it is not, however, a separate fallacy (*ābhāsa*). As for what Bhāsarvajña stated—"A reason that does not prove the probandum (*sādhya*) while residing in the subject (*pakṣa*) itself is 'unascertained' (*anadhyavasita*); for example, 'the earth is eternal because it possesses odor,' and 'everything is momentary because it exists,' etc."—among these, the first type is simply the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) [inconclusive] reason.

However, in the case of the argument "everything is momentary because it exists," since everything has been made the subject (*pakṣa*), there exists nothing that could serve as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) or a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). Consequently, neither positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) can be stated; thus, this is simply a failure to establish pervasion (*vyāpty-asiddhi*), and not another type of fallacy. Let this suffice. Therefore, the classification of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) is exactly as we have stated it. Now, for the fallacies of the example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*): That which is the locus for the comprehension of the pervasion between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is called an "illustration" (*udāharaṇa*) or an "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*). (Verse 883)

That [inference] is of two kinds, distinguished by similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Among these, *sādharmya* is the demonstration of the concomitance (*anvaya*) of the probans with the probandum; for example: "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, as in a kitchen. *Vaidharmya* is the demonstration of the concomitance of the absence of the probans with the absence of the probandum; for example: "Whatever does not possess fire does not possess smoke, as in a lake."

There are four fallacious examples (*sādhya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), namely: lacking the probandum (*sādhyahīna*), lacking the probans (*sādhanahīna*), lacking both (*ubhayahīna*), and lacking a locus (*āśrayahīna*). For example: "Sound is eternal because it is causeless; whatever is causeless is eternal. In this case, [the example] "like prior non-existence" (*prāgabhāva*) lacks the probandum; "like destruction" (*pradhvaṃsa*) lacks the probans; "like a jar" (*ghaṭa*) lacks both; and "like a human horn" (*naraśṛṅga*) lacks a locus. Here, "eternality" (*nityatva*) is intended to mean simply "indestructibility," not the absence of both extremes [of existence and non-existence].

The fallacious examples (*udāharaṇābhāsa*) are also fourfold, beginning with those that do not exclude the probandum (*sādhyāvyāvṛtta*). For instance: in the argument "whatever is not eternal is not causeless," the example "like destruction" (*pradhvaṃsa*) is one where the probandum is not excluded; "like prior non-existence" (*prāgabhāva*) is one where the probans is not excluded; "like space" (*gagana*) is one where both are not excluded; and "like a human horn" (*naraśṛṅga*) is one that lacks a locus (*āśrayahīna*). In both types of these examples, there are two faults: the statement of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) and the statement of inverse pervasion (*viparītavyāpti*).

In that regard, when one says merely, "The mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke, like a kitchen," this constitutes the statement of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*), because the pervasion—"whatever possesses smoke possesses fire"—has not been stated. Similarly, even if one says merely, "like a great lake," while failing to state the pervasion—"whatever does not possess fire does not possess smoke"—this also constitutes the statement of non-pervasion.

Furthermore, when, instead of saying "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire," one says "whatever possesses fire possesses smoke," this constitutes the statement of inverted pervasion (*viparīta-vyāpti*). It is exactly the same in the other case.
Since there is no possibility of [the reason] being absent in the subject (*pakṣa*), there are here two alternatives regarding the nature of the connection with the probandum (*sādhya*):

one must state that "whatever is not possessed of fire is not possessed of smoke," and this should be understood even when the formulation is "whatever is not possessed of smoke is not possessed of fire.
This elaboration on inference has been explained in many ways by many; however, it has been presented here by me according to the method taught by Citānanda. (89)

Thus ends the examination of inference within the section on the determination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the arising of [the view] consisting of pride; now follows the examination of verbal testimony (*śabda*).
Those learned in logic describe analogy after inference; however, we place verbal testimony (śabda) first because of its extensive acceptance by disputants. (90)

In that regard, when the recollection of word-meanings has been produced by means of cool words, the cognition of the sentence-meaning—which is not [otherwise] present to the senses—is called verbal (śābda). || 913 ||

This verbal knowledge depends upon linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*); therefore, we shall first demonstrate its method. A child, indeed, having observed the activity or joy of someone following sentences such as "Bring the cow" or "A son is born to you," and realizing that these two arise from prior cognition—specifically, that his activity and joy occurred only after a cognition of the objects such as bringing the cow or the birth of a son—and further realizing that such a cognition of the object arose immediately after the words "Bring the cow" and so forth, [concludes] that the word "Bring the cow" and the like...

One understands that [the word] conveys a meaning such as the bringing of a cow; at that time, the word is known as a single integrated unit (*piṇḍita*) as the conveyor of a single integrated meaning. Subsequently, in other usages such as "Bind the cow" (*gāṃ badhāna*) and "Bring the horse" (*aśvam ānaya*), one observes the processes of insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*apoha*)—namely, the addition and removal of other words—and thereby determines the distinction between word-meanings, such as: "The word *go* denotes that which possesses a dewlap and so forth," and "The word *ānaya* denotes the act of bringing."

Regarding this, Pārthasārathi and others maintain that the cognition of word-meanings by means of words is indeed *abhidhāna* (denotation), because it is produced by the power (*śakti*) of the word. On the other hand, Citānanda and others hold that since a word also causes the cognition of word-meanings only through the awakening of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), the knowledge of word-meanings is strictly a matter of memory (*smaraṇa*). Thus, although the meanings of individual words are restricted from the very beginning, their capacity for conveying the knowledge of a single qualified meaning (*viśiṣṭārtha*)—as observed from the outset—remains intact.

Thus, when the knowledge of word-meanings (*padārtha*) has been established, there subsequently arises the knowledge of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), which consists in the cognition of various qualified objects. Regarding the inquiry as to whether this is produced by the words themselves or by the recollections of the word-meanings, the view common to the Naiyāyikas and others is as follows: since the words have exhausted their function in conveying the word-meanings and because they are [thereby] separated [from the final cognition], it is the word-meanings themselves that convey the sentence-meaning in the form of their own mutual relations.

We, however, maintain that word-meanings (padārthas) themselves convey the sentence-meaning through indication (lakṣaṇā). For indication occurs precisely because the literal meaning (vācyārtha) is untenable. In this case, if the word-meanings such as "cow" and so forth, being merely recalled by the words, were to remain in their general form alone without mutual connection, then the intention of the words—determined at the time of linguistic convention—to convey a single qualified object would be contradicted. Thus, due to the untenability of the general form as the literal meaning, the word-meanings must reside in the specific [relation] consisting of mutual connection.

They culminate [in this]. Consequently, "this cow" is understood as being brought, and the act of bringing is understood as being connected specifically to the cow; thus, through the attainment of mutual connection (*parasparānvaya*), the sentence-meaning in the form of "the bringing of the cow" is established. Therefore, in this case, the word-meanings, having been first cognized by the words, subsequently enter into mutual connection. In this manner, the doctrine of *abhihitānvaya* (the connection of what has been expressed) has been demonstrated for people such as ourselves.

The theory of "expression of the related" (anvitābhidhāna) held by others is that all words express their own meanings as already connected with the meanings of other words once the completion of all the other words has occurred. (933)

For upon the first hearing of the command "Bring the cow," it is the word itself that is known as the signifier of the related meaning consisting of the bringing of the cow. Therefore, in accordance with that, one must again maintain that it is the words themselves—and not the word-meanings—that possess the capacity to signify the related meaning. Indeed, even when word-meanings are being isolated through the process of insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*apoha*), it is observed that in each instance those meanings appear only as related to this or that [other meaning], and never in isolation; thus, the power of words to signify their own meanings as related (*anvita*) is not abandoned.

Now, is it not the case that there is no understanding of isolated word-meanings at all from words? We say: there is. To begin with, words do indeed cause the recollection of their respective meanings individually; however, they do not stop there. Rather, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that they cease only after expressing each of their own recalled meanings once again as being connected with the meanings of the other words. Therefore, the sentence-meaning, which consists of the related form, is indeed what is expressed by the words themselves, and not something merely understood through the word-meanings.

Furthermore, if [the sentence-meaning] were understood through the word-meanings, then there would be a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) even with those word-meanings apprehended by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), yet such a thing is not observed. Thus, this doctrine of the Guru (Prabhākara) is to be rejected precisely because of its complexity (*gaurava*). For in our view, since word-meanings are established through memory and the sentence-meaning is established through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), there is no need to postulate an additional power (*śakti*); thus, it is you yourselves who have incurred complexity by proposing the postulation of a power in words. Moreover, the power residing in word-meanings is indeed simpler than the power residing in words.

In that case, if it is postulated that a single object, namely "going" (*gamana*), conveys the syntactic connection (*anvaya*), then the connection of other synonyms for "going" is also established. However, regarding word-potency (*pada-śakti*), one would have to postulate the potency of infinite words whose meanings are "going," which entails great complexity (*mahā-gaurava*). Furthermore, if in a single sentence every word were to convey its own meaning as connected with the others individually, it would follow—by force of logic—that the meaning of the entire sentence would be cognized at every single word; thus, this [theory] is even more difficult to maintain.

As for the objection that if words were to convey the syntactic connection (anvaya) of objects, then even those objects apprehended through other means of knowledge would enter into such a connection—we reply as follows: Even according to your own view, when it is said, "Bind the cow," why does the horse—which is seen nearby, has its halter removed, and stands in need of being bound—not enter into a connection with the act of binding? In that case, you must necessarily admit that the horse lacks such a connection simply because it was not apprehended through the word.

And so, in that very same way, even for those things apprehended by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), non-connection is established precisely because they lack the status of being apprehended by words; thus, in that case as well, nothing further need be postulated by us. Therefore, the method of connection stated by us alone is the simpler one.
In this regard, expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatva*), and proximity (*sannidhi*)—these three—are postulated as the causes for the comprehension of the meaning of every sentence. (943)

In cases such as "a fair-skinned horse," "a man," or "an elephant," where there is no mutual expectancy, no syntactic connection is observed; therefore, expectancy is first of all accepted [as a necessary condition for verbal cognition]. (953)

Because there is no syntactic connection with what is semantically incompatible—as in the case of "he sprinkles with fire"—semantic competency (*yogyatā*) must also be accepted as a requirement; next, proximity (*sannidhi*) is explained. (963)

The "proximity" (*sannidhi*) of word-meanings is defined as their being understood by words as being present together. Therefore, the absence of proximity occurs in two ways: through the absence of presence and through the absence of being understood by words. In that regard, there is a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) between the two words "cow" (*gām*) and "bring" (*ānaya*) when they are uttered at different times, because they lack proximity. In the case of "bind the cow" (*gāṃ badhāna*), there is likewise a lack of connection because the horse, which is seen and requires binding, lacks the quality of being understood by words.

Therefore, the rule that concomitance (*anvaya*) occurs only between those things understood through words is established. However, the Guru maintains that "proximity" (*sannidhi*) consists merely in the presence of [an object] in the mind, and not in verbal proximity. As was stated previously, even he—being unable to prevent the concomitance of a horse in the sentence "Tie up the cow"—will have to reluctantly accept that concomitance occurs only between those things expressed by words. Now, one might object: "In that case, let the horse not be concomitant simply because the sentence lacks *tātparya* (intentional focus) toward the horse, and not because of its lack of verbal status. This is not so.

Likewise, in cases such as "one should sprinkle with fire," there is a lack of syntactic connection precisely because of the absence of *tātparya* (intentional meaning); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of not even accepting [the requirements of] semantic competency (*yogyatva*) and so forth.
Therefore, *tātparya* is never itself a cause for the establishment of syntactic connection;
rather, it is sought again only for the purpose of restriction when other causal complexes are present. (973)
Such is the established position.
Thus, because there is no other possibility, even the Guru has accepted that the relation belongs only to words; this lack of restriction [regarding the nature of the relation] now stands. (983)
Therefore, the twofold assistance previously mentioned by us—that there would be no other [means of knowledge] for those things already cognized by another means of knowledge—is established. (991)

Even in cases such as "the door," there will be an ellipsis [of a verb], because it is only a verbal element that can serve as the basis for syntactic connection (anvaya), as in the thought, "Let the door be closed. (1003)
"The word alone must be supplied"—this is the view of those like me;
however, the Teacher desires that the meaning of the ellipsis be supplied there. (1013)
Out of the vain hope that it might also follow from the giver of the instruction, this teacher, being arrogant, teaches exactly what he himself has been taught. (1023)
"In that case, it will certainly roar: 'The supplying of a meaning [from outside the text]! (103)

Let this matter rest for now. The manner of knowing the meaning of a sentence has already been explained. It was stated that verbal cognition (*śābda*) is the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence whose referent is not present to the senses. This very [cognition] is also called *āgama* (tradition/scripture). Furthermore, by the term "not present" (*asannikṛṣṭa*), the lack of authority of those sentences which are mere restatements (*anuvāda*) or those whose meanings are sublated is indicated. That verbal cognition is of two kinds: human (*pauruṣeya*) and non-human (*apauruṣeya*). Among these, the word of a reliable person (*āpta*) is human, while the word of the Veda is non-human. But the Teacher says: "Verbal cognition exists only in the form of the Veda."

Human utterances, however, are merely indicators of the speaker’s intention; they do not themselves convey the meaning of the sentence, because their power is blunted by doubt. Although words possess the capacity for conveying meaning established at the time of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*), that capacity becomes blunted in the case of human statements—which abound in deviation—due to the constant apprehension of such doubt.

In that regard, as long as it is not inferred that the speaker uttered the sentence only after having understood this crooked meaning, the suspicion of its being otherwise does not cease; thus, the sentence remains indifferent [to its own truth]. Likewise, since the intention (*tātparya*) of human speech is dependent upon the speaker's cognition, the sentence also remains indifferent because the intention cannot be determined without the inference of the speaker’s cognition. Therefore, the speaker’s cognition must first be inferred.

In this regard, when the sentence "There are fruits on the bank of the river" is heard and the individual word-meanings are recalled separately, one infers: "These words were employed only after cognizing the connection between these word-meanings, because they are words uttered by a reliable person, just like the words 'Bring the cow'.

Thus, the listener, having exerted effort to understand the speaker's knowledge of the connection between the word-meanings, necessarily arrives at the sentence-meaning in the form of that connection between the word-meanings; therefore, in the speech of humans, the sentence-meaning is indeed inferable.
Thus, when the fear of deviation has vanished and the determination of the sentence-meaning has arisen, the word speaks again as a mere restatement; such is his (Śabara’s) conclusion. (104)
This is improper:
disregarding even the suspicion of deviation, is a sequence of words not capable of expressing its own object, just like the sense organs and so forth? (105)

The intended meaning is also easily understood by itself, without the inference of [the author's] knowledge, as it is in the Veda and as it is in other works whose authors have not been considered. (106)
And if you maintain that [the proof] ends with the inference of the speaker’s cognition, then, since that too is impossible, what will you do with your shattered hopes? (107)

Indeed, the quality of being composed by a reliable person (*āpta*) is stated here as the reason. And reliability is intended as the absence of error and the like. It is impossible to determine in any instance that "this person has no error at all," because it has been said: "Error is suspected even in the case of the seers (*ṛṣis*); how much more so, then, in the case of those belonging to later times? Likewise, it is equally difficult to determine that "he has no error in this particular place or time."

Therefore, since this person has no error regarding the meaning of the sentence in question, it is only after first knowing the meaning of the sentence that error can be removed. Consequently, prior to the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, the speaker’s reliability (*āptatva*) is unestablished; how then could it be inferred by him? Thus, the doctrine of the Guru (Prabhākara) is destroyed. In this way, by precluding the status of inference for worldly words, even those who maintain that all verbal cognition is inference are frustrated. (108)

Indeed, the followers of Kaṇāda and others, being of limited intellect, assert that all sentence-meanings are inferable solely by way of what has been stated by their teachers; they too must be refuted by this very [argument]. For even by them, the sentence-meaning must be inferred through reasons such as "being a faultless statement" and so forth. Furthermore, "faultlessness" consists in the absence of error and the like, and that must be determined only after the sentence-meaning itself has been determined. Thus, according to the method previously described, for them as well, the reason remains unestablished (*asiddha*). Let this suffice for now. Therefore, in this manner, verbal cognition—both worldly and Vedic—is established. In that regard:
When the defect of being composed by a wicked speaker occurs in a word, then there may also be deviation in some human utterances. (109)
But in the case of the Veda, which is not of human origin, no blemish arising from contact with a person can be suspected; how, then, could there be any lack of reliability? (110)

The Vedic [scripture] is manifold, being divided by the distinctions of injunctions (vidhi), mantras, and explanatory passages (arthavāda), as well as by the distinctions between direct instruction (upadeśa) and extended application (atideśa); however, since such matters cannot be made known through a limited discussion, we shall desist.
Thus ends the examination of verbal testimony (śābda) in the section on the means of knowledge (pramāṇa-pariccheda) in the *Mānameyodaya*.
Now follows the examination of comparison (upamāna).

Comparison (upamiti) is held to be the cognition of similarity with respect to an object not present [to the senses], which has as its domain an object being remembered due to the similarity with an object currently being perceived.

Just as, after perceiving the similarity of a cow in a gavaya, there arises the cognition of the similarity of the gavaya in the cow being remembered; for instance, even though one has previously seen a cow in the city, its similarity to a gavaya does not manifest, because the gavaya itself has not been observed. (112)
But when, having reached the forest at some time, one perceives a gavaya, then the similarity between that [gavaya] and the cow should be grasped by perception itself. (113)
Furthermore, when only a cow standing at a distance appears to him, what indeed could be the cause for the similarity with a gavaya to manifest there as well? (114)
For that [object] was not previously grasped such that it could now be remembered;
if it is argued that it is not grasped by perception now because of its distance, [the response follows]. || 115 ||
And since it appears clearly, another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is sought;
regarding that, the followers of Śabara and the followers of Śaṅkara have declared it to be analogy (upamāna). (116)

In this regard, let it be understood that the perception of similarity residing in the gavaya is the instrument (karaṇa), while the cognition of similarity residing in the cow is the result (phala). || 117 ||

The logicians, however, seeking a different kind of analogy (*upamāna*), attempt to reduce the cognition of similarity residing in the cow to inference (*anumāna*). For instance: "Whatever is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the similarity residing in X is similar to that [X] as well; for example, one palm is similar to another palm. And the cow is the counter-correlative of the similarity residing in the *gavaya*. Therefore, it is similar to the *gavaya* as well. This is incorrect.

For in this case, when one infers by means of a mere general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*)—namely, that "whatever is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of a similarity residing in something is similar to that thing as well"—only this much appears: "there is some similarity," just as [one might infer] "there is some fire. However, the specific similarity of a cow to a *gavaya* would not be determined clearly and definitively, as it is in perception. Therefore, because we observe a definitive determination [of the specific object], this is not an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). Consequently, since it is not an inference, it is indeed a distinct means of knowledge (*mānāntara*).

But surely, at that very time, just as there is a clear appearance of the cow’s similarity to the gavaya, there is also a clear appearance of the man’s dissimilarity to the gavaya. In that case too, why is another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) resorted to? We reply: it is not so. For in that instance, the man’s dissimilarity—which consists in the absence of the properties residing in the gavaya—is understood precisely through the means of valid cognition known as non-apprehension (*abhāva*); what need is there for another means of valid cognition? However, the logicians (*tārkika*) have proposed comparison (*upamāna*) as something distinct.

Suppose someone who has come from the city asks a forest-dweller, "What is this animal called a *gavaya*? Having heard the analogical statement (atideśavākya) that "a *gavaya* is like a cow," he goes back to the forest and, upon seeing a particular kind of deer, recognizes it, thinking, "This is indeed that which is like a cow. Thereafter, he also understands the connection between the name and the named object, thinking, "This very animal is a *gavaya*. This apprehension of the connection is *upamiti* (analogical cognition). Its instrument—the recognition of the meaning of the [analogical] statement—is *upamāna* (analogy).

Furthermore, this apprehension of the relationship is not to be accomplished by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For previously, at the time of hearing the sentence, because the gavaya—the bearer of the name—had not been seen, it was impossible to establish the connection there. But when the gavaya is being perceived, the sentence has already passed away; thus, the sentence lacks the capacity to bring about that cognition. [Objection: However, it was already understood from the sentence that the word "gavaya" is applied to an individual body resembling a cow.

"Based on that perceived gavaya, let it be inferred: 'The word *gavaya* is the designator (*vācaka*) of this [animal], because it is employed here without [the presence of] secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth, just as the word 'cow' is the designator of a cow. This too is incorrect. For in that case, only the mere fact of its being employed is understood from the sentence; however, the absence of secondary indication and so forth is difficult to ascertain prior to the establishment of its status as a designator. Thus, this reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*). Therefore, this knowledge of the relationship is indeed to be accomplished by means of analogy (*upamāna*). "Analogy is declared to arise from the meaning of the sentence concerning similarity. (118)

In this very way, indeed, [the cognition] may arise from dissimilarity and from the mere property [of being a horse], just as the notion "this is a horse" [arises] because it has two hooves, unlike cows and other such animals. (119)
Having thus understood the meaning of the statement regarding dissimilarity (vaidharmya), one who has gone to another country perceives a single-hoofed animal and recognizes it as a horse.
In exactly the same way, when only the property (dharma) is heard, there sometimes arises a cognition of a relation [between it and a subject], such as:
"The camel has a long neck, hanging lips, and eats thorns. (121)
Having heard this, they then recognize the camel elsewhere;
in this way, [the object is cognized] through the distinction between the properties of similarity, dissimilarity, and the mere property itself. (122)
"The meaning of the sentence of transfer is threefold; therefore, analogy is of three kinds.
(1223) This ill-conceived view is to be rejected, because this cognition of the relationship is produced solely by verbal cognition supported by perception. (1233)
For when a person asks, "What is a *gavaya*?", the intention of the reply, "A *gavaya* is like a cow," is understood to be solely the demonstration of the referent denoted by the word *gavaya*.
Therefore, a word does not reach its completion without demonstrating its denoted referent;
and prior to the cognition of a *gavaya*, such a demonstration is impossible. (1243)

Consequently, the sentence, its intended meaning (tātparya) not yet understood and thus remaining incomplete, becomes fully realized in its purpose only at the moment the gavaya is perceived; having been recalled from memory as that whose denotable object is now demonstrated by perception, it then brings about the cognition of the relationship between the name and the named.

Just as a merchant, upon hearing the statement "the new woolen blanket is [for sale]," approaches the marketplace and, seeing nine blankets, understands the meaning of the sentence by grasping the intended focus on the specific number, so too should it be understood here. Therefore, since the acquisition of the relationship (*saṅgatigrahaṇa*) is accomplished solely through verbal testimony aided by perception, no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) need be sought.

Furthermore, the term "analogy" (*upamāna*) is well-known in the world as referring to similarity; how then could its application to dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) or to a mere property (*dharmamātra*) be possible for you? (1253)
"Likewise, the word 'atideśa' (extended application) is well-known in a sentence that conveys similarity;
even that, when mentioned in another context, pains me.
Therefore, we [accept] only the cognition of similarity residing in the cow as our sole refuge.
We accept analogy as a means of valid cognition; by this, even those who maintain that there are only three means of knowledge are defeated. ||127||
In this matter of similarity, we have a dispute with our teacher;
for the teacher considers this similarity to be an entirely distinct category of entity. (1283)
We maintain that a universal is a collection of qualities and so forth; its specific nature will be discussed somewhat when the occasion for the categories arises. (1293)

Thus ends the examination of analogy (*upamāna*) in the section on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within the *Mānameyodaya*. Now follows the examination of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

The definition of presumption (arthāpatti) as stated in the Bhāṣya is simply this: it is the postulation of that which makes something else possible, based on the impossibility [of the observed fact] otherwise. (1303)
In that context, the contradiction between two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is called "inconsistency" (anupapatti).
Therefore, one should learn the definition [of presumption] from the perspective of what is unique to the means of valid cognition, as distinct from those common to all.
When there is no contradiction, the cognition regarding the non-contradictory portion is accepted as presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). || 1311 ||

Just as for one who is known to be alive, the postulation of his being outside [the house] arises from the contradiction caused by the means of knowledge consisting in the absence [of him] in the house.

(132) By means of an inference based on calculation and scripture, it is understood in a general sense that Devadatta is alive somewhere, either in the house or outside; when there is a contradiction with the statement "he is not in the house," in order to resolve that contradiction, it is postulated that he is outside. This is the cognition of presumption (*arthāpatti*), which has the function of resolving the contradiction between two means of valid cognition.
"Desiring to establish that this [non-apprehension] is indeed inference, the logicians have declared:
'There is no contradiction between two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and even in the case of what is well-known, such [contradiction] is equal [to non-contradiction].

(1333) Thus, first of all, a contradiction between two means of valid cognition is impossible; for if it were so, as in the case of 'this is silver' and 'this is not silver,' it would follow that one of them is invalid. If it is argued that nevertheless a contradiction is observed between the stated means of valid cognition, that too is mere wishful thinking. For here, by the means of valid cognition consisting in the non-existence in the house, there occurs a sublation (bādha) only of a specific location which was the very object of doubt—namely, whether [the person] is in the house or outside."

For by the means of knowledge consisting of "living," only living itself, or its connection with a general location, is made the object; however, neither of these two is touched upon or even reached by the means of knowledge consisting of "absence from home. Therefore, since there is no contradiction at all between the means of knowledge of "living" and "absence from home," how can it be said that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) arises through that [means] acting as an instrument?
Furthermore, since such a contradiction is possible even in well-known inferences, the entire web of inference would overflow into the domain of presumptive testimony. (Verse 1343)

By means of the valid cognition that apprehends the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, "where there is smoke, there is fire"—fire is established on the mountain as well; or else, the smoke being observed on the mountain implies its own cause, fire. Thus, by either the valid cognition apprehending the pervasion or by the observation of smoke, it is understood that fire exists somewhere on the mountain. Since this fire is not perceived in the upper part of the mountain, its presence in the lower part is postulated due to the contradiction [otherwise]. Consequently, this would result in the fallacy of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Therefore, this [instance] must be included within the category of inference (*anumāna*).

And thus it is inferred: "Devadatta exists outside, because while being alive, he is not in the house; for whoever is alive and is not in a certain place must exist elsewhere, just as I do. Therefore, this fifth means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is refuted. This is what we teach: there is indeed a contradiction between the two means of knowledge;
there is no subversion of a well-established inference, nor is there an inference regarding external existence [that would override it]. (1353)

Regarding what was stated there—that when two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are in conflict, one must be invalid—this is indeed a case of conflict between two unique means of valid cognition, such as "this is silver" and "this is not silver. However, even when a common means of valid cognition is sublated by a unique means of valid cognition, its invalidity does not arise, because it still possesses scope [for application]. (1363)

Therefore, a contradiction between the two means of valid cognition is indeed possible. As for what was further stated—that here too, it is only a specific location that is sublated when it is doubtful, and not the means of valid cognition regarding life—we reply:
"When Devadatta’s being alive is known through inference, his connection with a location must also be known for the sake of establishing his continued existence. (1373)
If, in that case, the mere generality of being a location were connected [to the person], then by virtue of that connection with location, this person too would be a location. (138)
Consequently, his life is known to depend upon a universal that is not restricted to a specific individual or location, such that one knows, "He is living somewhere. (1393)
Therefore, even when there is doubt as to whether [the person] is at home or outside, the living state is indeed cognized only by relying upon some particular characteristic. (1403)
In that case, if one particular [part] were sublated, then prior to the apprehension of another,
the cognition of living would itself be sublated, being devoid of any objective basis.

Thus, before the external existence [of the object] has been established, those who do not perceive the subtle state of contradiction arising from the apprehension of its absence in the house speak as they do. (1423)

Thus it is said. As for the claim that even well-known inferences would have to be considered *arthāpatti* (presumption), that too is not correct. For in those cases, one must state what the common means of valid cognition (*sādhāraṇapramāṇa*) is that establishes the presence of fire on the mountain. If you say, "By the very means of cognition that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*), fire is established on the mountain as well," then alas! Who is this person, kissing the back of a Prābhākara, who has uttered such nonsense?
How could one who had not previously seen the mountain understand its possession of fire? Thus, their view regarding inference is also destroyed. (1433)

As for what was further stated—that smoke implies its own cause, fire—what is the meaning of that? Ah, it must be explained as "smoke causes one to infer fire. Consequently, it is inference alone, which brings about the cognition of fire on the mountain, that has been described there as the primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, there is no subversion of inference. And when that [inference] is sublated by the non-perception of upward [smoke], the postulation of [fire] below follows.

"It is accepted as being merely a case of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti); alas, there is nothing [else] at all. (1443) Furthermore, that inference which has been employed by you to establish external existence is unestablished in its very nature (*svarūpāsiddha*) for your long-lived selves. This is because it is impossible to define mere living without qualification. Prior to the apprehension of external existence, one cannot cognize both "living" and "absence from the house" in combination. Therefore, since the probans (*liṅga*)—which consists of the absence from the house qualified by living—is not perceived, this reason is unestablished due to ignorance of its own nature.

As it is stated in the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*: "Therefore, that absence of [the person] in the house which is perceived of one who is alive is the probans; and that [absence] is not apprehended without having apprehended his existence outside. Thus, presumption (*arthāpatti*) is indeed a distinct means of knowledge.
By one who does not know such a method for the destruction of the Logicians (*Tārkika*), the Teacher has instead prattled about the doubt regarding [the person's] being alive in this context. (1453)
Indeed, life was previously known only through its presence within the house; therefore, doubt regarding life arises from not seeing it in the house. (1463)
This life, though itself uncertain, serves as a means of cognition for the existence of something external;
this is the power of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), in that it brings about cognition even when it is itself doubtful. (1473)
Thus, when there is doubt regarding existence, the reason would possess a doubtful qualification; in this case, the refutation of its status as an inference is easily accomplished for us. (1483)
This is laughable.
For instance: "If life is in doubt due to the observation of the absence from home, then its determination must be made again by means of the testimony of a reliable person and so forth. (1493)
Or, by observing signs such as the necklace around her beloved’s neck, nothing at all is requested from him; therefore, there is no doubt whatsoever. ||1503||
Furthermore, there is no apprehension of an external object because life is uncertain;
when there is even a suspicion of death, how can there be the cognition that "it exists outside"? (1513)
"Whether he lives or not, therefore he remains outside"—who else besides the Guru is capable of conceiving such a notion? (1523)

If it is argued that everything is possible through the power of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), then alas, since all things are not perceived, there would be doubt regarding their destruction. (1533)
Having ascertained that it exists elsewhere, let the mind be made satisfied;
therefore, doubtfulness is not a cause for presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). 1543.

Thus, presumption (*arthāpatti*) is of the kind we have described. Furthermore, it is twofold: presumption from what is perceived (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*) and presumption from what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*). Among these, presumption from what is perceived has been explained.
However, where a word is supplied (*adhyāhriyate*) in order to establish the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of an incomplete sentence, there presumption from what is heard is intended. (Verse 1553)

For example, in the sentence "the door, the door," there is a common means of knowledge (*sādhāraṇapramāṇa*) which dictates that for the sake of establishing syntactic connection (*anvaya*), there must be some other meaning such as "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) understood through the word. When this [general requirement] is sublated by the non-perception of the heard word [in its specific sense], one must postulate a meaning such as "obstruction" as something not conveyed by the heard word. In that case, one who is intent on postulating a meaning such as "obstruction" along with the word itself, because the understanding of the meaning is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) when derived from the word alone, postulates the word itself. This is *śrutārthāpatti*, which consists in the postulation of a word.

The Teacher, however, states that there is no presumption based on the literal meaning (*śrutārthāpatti*), because [in the case of *arthāpatti*] one merely postulates a meaning such as "obscuration" and the like, whereas here there is no postulation of a word. But that [objection] has already been silenced, since it is established that the connection [of the word] is proven only by means of a word already understood through scripture. Furthermore, if the meaning alone were to be postulated for the purpose of completing the sentence, then in cases such as "I offer what is pleasing to Sūrya," it would be the meaning in the form of Sūrya himself that must be supplied, rather than the postulation of the word "to Sūrya" (*sūryāya*).

[Objection: But surely, since this element is seen to be presented by a word in the archetype (*prakṛti*), a word must also be postulated for it in the ectype (*vikṛti*). [Reply: Not so. For ritual elements are not drawn over into the ectype merely because they are seen there; rather, they are drawn over only for a specific purpose. Furthermore, you have no need for that element to be conveyed by a word, since its syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is established even otherwise.

If apprehension were based on mere observation, then since another instance of a preparatory act (*saṃskāra*) has been observed in the case of what has already been threshed, threshing itself would have to be performed even upon the *kṛṣṇala* grains. Therefore, the establishment of presumption (*ūha*) occurs through presumptive testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*) alone; let this matter rest here.
Thus ends the examination of presumption in the "Examination of the Means and Objects of Knowledge" section of the *Mānameyodaya*. Now follows the examination of non-existence (*abhāva*).
Now, the examination of non-existence:

Furthermore, when there is non-perception despite the presence of conditions for perceptibility, that which is called the means of valid cognition known as "non-existence" (abhāva) would be the indicator of non-existence. (1563)

For in this case, non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*). And since that [non-apprehension] consists in the absence of cognition, it is called a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the form of a non-existence (*abhāva*). In that regard: "Indeed, capacity (*yogyatā*) is the perfection of the causal complex (*sāmagrīsampatti*) for apprehension, even in the absence of an object and those [factors] dependent upon it, such as sense-object contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) and so forth. (Verse 1571)
And that [non-apprehension] is a cooperative cause for the cognition of absence through its being known;
however, non-apprehension when unknown makes [the absence] known by its mere existence. (1583)

Therefore, when one realizes that all the causes for perceiving a jar—which is the object—such as the opening of the eyes, the arrival of light, and the application of the mind, along with the sensory contact (*indriya-sannikarṣa*) and so forth dependent upon them, have arisen at this very moment, then the non-perception of the jar, aided by these factors, makes known the absence of the jar; this is how it should be understood in all cases. Indeed, for the sake of discerning fitness (*yogyatva*), one exerts effort toward the arrival of the rays of the eye capable of perceiving subtle objects, in order to know the absence of such subtle things. (Verse 1593)
When there is doubt or even error regarding fitness, there is indeed doubt or delusion regarding its non-existence as well; for example: [16]
Searching for his ring with both hands in the darkness,
he falls into doubt even when it is absent, because of the uncertainty caused by the touch of the entire earth.
In the same way, having perceived the absence of touch everywhere as a universal contact,
one perceives through delusion the non-existence of even a ring that actually exists.

Therefore, the determination of fitness (*yogyatva*) is the auxiliary factor here. Non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), moreover, is of two kinds: consisting in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) and consisting in the absence of memory (*smaraṇābhāva*). Among these, it has been stated that the knowledge of the non-existence of a jar and so forth arises from non-apprehension in the form of the absence of the means of perception (*pratyakṣa*). Similarly, in the apprehension of the non-existence of objects cognizable through inference, the non-arising of a competent inference should be understood as the indicator.

As it has been stated by Manorathanandin—that the non-arising of an inference based on the mark of activity (ceṣṭāliṅgaka), which would otherwise indicate the perception of form, indicates the owl’s absence of perception of form during the day—so it is with other means of valid cognition as well. For example, from the absence of memory, there arises at evening the cognition: "Maitra was not here this morning."

For in that case, since Maitra as qualified by the morning time is not capable of being perceived at evening, the very fact of his non-recollection—despite his being otherwise capable of being remembered—is relied upon as the indicator of the absence of Maitra as qualified by the morning time at that moment. However, the logicians (Tārkikas), asserting that absence is cognizable through perception and other means, do not accept that it is cognizable solely through non-apprehension (anupalambha). That is incorrect.

For they too, since the cognition of the absence [of an object] at the morning time during the evening lacks the quality of being produced by the senses, would necessarily have to accept, by the reasoning already stated, that it arises solely from non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). [Objection: But surely, in that case, the existence [of the object] at the morning time is indeed inferred by means of the mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the absence of memory, as seen in the *Meyodaya*. [Reply: Not so. Because the absence of memory cannot be known; for the logicians (*tārkika*) indeed maintain that the absence of recollection is grasped by the mind (*manas*).
And that is incorrect, for we, at least, are proponents of the theory that cognition is not directly perceived (*jñānāpratyakṣavādin*).
"We deny that cognitions are accessible through mental perception (*manasa-pratyakṣa*);
and consequently, how could their non-existence also be grasped by the mind? (1643). [Objection:
But we infer the perceptibility of non-existence. This very point has been stated by him [the author]: "Because the cognition is immediate and because the sense organ is not exhausted..."

"And because it is made unknown [by the mind], and because the mind is absorbed in the positive entity," and so forth. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "Non-existence is perceptible, because it is cognized non-mediately (*aparokṣa*), like a jar. In this regard, the reason is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), because non-existence lacks the quality of being cognized non-mediately. Since the ground (*bhūtala*) and so forth are cognized non-mediately, your confusion regarding non-existence is merely a delusion that the non-existence itself is likewise [non-mediately perceived]. [Objection: "But the cognition of non-existence is perception, because it is produced by the senses which have not ceased their function, like the cognition of a jar. [Response: That too is unestablished in its qualification (*viśeṣāsiddha*). For, in this case, the sense organ has already ceased its function once the aforementioned capacity (*yogyatā*) has been established.
Even by logicians, capacity must be accepted for the sake of understanding non-existence. (1653)
"If a jar were present here, it would be perceived, just like the ground"—by means of such reasoning, they too apprehend precisely the condition of perceptibility. (1663)
Let the meaning of the statement "if it existed, it would be perceived" be investigated: does it mean that everything other than the jar here has become a cause of cognition? (1673)
The term *viśeṣa* means a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, as for the argument that "the cognition of absence is perceptual because its cause is not known, like the cognition of a jar or similar objects," that is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to memory;
for the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is the cause of memory, and it brings about cognition while remaining unknown.
"Even though its cause is unknown, memory thus attains the status of perception.

(1683) Furthermore, as for the argument that "the cognition of absence is produced by a mind permeated by a cause in the form of a positive entity, because it is a cognition, like other cognitions; therefore, it is not logical for non-apprehension to be its cause"—that too is incorrect. For one could equally say: "The cognition of absence has a cause other than the sense organs, because it is a cognition of absence, like the cognition of an absence inferred [through other means]."

As for the argument that the cognition of non-existence has the sense organ as its instrument because it is corrupted by a defect of the sense organ—just as the cognition of color, being corrupted by a defect of the eye, has the eye as its instrument—that too is unproven.
Indeed, a defect of the sense organ cannot be the cause of the error regarding non-existence;
rather, it has been stated that in this case, the cause is simply the error regarding the object's fitness [for perception]. (Verse 1691)

Furthermore, as for other inferences such as "the eye is a perceiver of non-existence because it is a sense faculty, like the mind," all of them are contradicted by a specific counter-thesis (*viśeṣaviruddha*). This is because a sense faculty perceives only that which is related to it, and since a relation cannot be admitted in the case of non-existence, and because a relation in the form of a qualifier-qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*) relation is necessarily preceded by another underlying relation.

Moreover, the very capacity for a thing to be related to a sense faculty would be the limiting condition (*upādhi*) for its perceptibility; thus, all [such inferences] fail due to the non-establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*). (Verse 1701)

[Objection: Surely there exists a relation called the "qualifier-qualified" (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva) [between absence and its locus]. [Reply: Not so. For only if the perceptibility of absence were established could some relation, however difficult it might be, possibly exist; yet even that has not been established to this day. (1713)

Furthermore, since non-existence (*abhāva*)—being devoid of the relation of qualifier and qualified and lacking any other relation—is like Mount Meru and the Vindhya mountains [in being mutually unrelated], there is no status as qualifier or qualified here at all; how then can there be even a trace of "contact" (*saṃnikarṣa*) for that which is non-existent? Moreover:

"There would be no recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) at the outset in indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*); therefore, you must accept that the cognition of non-existence occurs only through determinate perception (*savikalpaka*). (1723)

Therefore, it is inferred as follows: non-existence is not perceptible, because it is unfit for indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), just like a supersensible object (*atīndriyavastu*). Thus, since the audacity of the Naiyāyikas has been refuted, it is established that non-existence is known solely through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). However, Prabhākara asserts that there is no such thing as an entity called "non-existence" at all; by this, he mocks those who concern themselves with the investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (Verse 1733)
We shall also refute that [objection] in the establishment of the categories of things (padārtha).
Thus, the sixfold system of valid cognition (ṣaṭpramāṇī) has been established without opposition.

But those who consider "origination" (sambhava) and "tradition" (aitihya) to be separate means of valid cognition have adopted the conduct of thieves regarding inference and verbal testimony. || 1753 ||
For instance, as for the argument that "the cognition of non-existence is perceptual because its cause is not known, like the cognition of a jar," that is inconclusive with respect to memory;
for the cause of memory is a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), and that is a cognizer even though it is itself unknown.
"Even though its instrument is unknown, memory thus does not attain the status of perception.

(1683) Furthermore, as for the argument that "the cognition of absence is produced by a mind permeated by an instrumental cause of a positive nature, because it is a cognition, like other cognitions; therefore, it is not logical for non-perception (*anupalambha*) to be its instrument"—that too is incorrect. For one could also say: "The cognition of absence has an instrument other than the sense organs, because it is a cognition of absence, like the cognition of an absence that is to be inferred (*anumeya*)."

As for the claim that the cognition of absence has the sense organ as its instrument because it is corrupted by a defect of the sense organ—just as the cognition of color, when corrupted by a defect of the eye, has the eye as its instrument—that too is unproven.
Indeed, a defect of the sense organ cannot be the cause of the error regarding absence;
rather, it is said that in this case, the error regarding the object's fitness (*yogyatā*) alone is the cause. (Verse 1691)

Furthermore, as for other inferences such as "the eye is a perceiver of absence because it is a sense faculty, like the mind," all of them are contradicted by the specific [conclusion] (viśeṣaviruddha), because a sense faculty can only be a perceiver of that which is related, and since no relation is admitted in the case of an absence, and because the relation consisting of the qualifier-qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva) is necessarily preceded by another relation.

Moreover, the very capacity of an object to be related to a sense faculty would be the limiting condition (upādhi) for its perceptibility; therefore, all [such inferences] fail due to the non-establishment of pervasion (vyāpti). (1701)
That which is the cognition of a hundred and so forth within numbers such as a thousand, and that which is the grasping of a *prastha* and so forth within measures such as a *khārī*; || 1761 ||
They say that its "origination" (sambhava) is the limit, for origination is indeed the end;
and those of pure mind maintain that this is a knowledge derived from inference. (1773)
First, because one observes the inclusion of "two" and so forth within "one," it is known that a smaller number is inherent in a larger number. (1783)
And therefore, through the cognition of pervasion, small numbers such as hundreds would be understood within thousands and so forth by means of the reason of being "more. (1793)
In the same way, even regarding measurements, the experience of the smaller from the larger is to be inferred;
thus, because the possibility of inference exists, [the category of] "possibility" (sambhava) is refuted.
A statement that relies solely on mere report is called tradition (aitihya), such as, "There is Vaiśravaṇa in every banyan tree," and so forth. || 1813 ||
That [tradition] is generally accepted as being non-authoritative due to its lack of a foundational source.
But if this is so, how indeed can the accounts of Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and others be authoritative for you? (1823)

Do not say so; for such [knowledge] is indeed verbal, since it arises from the established authority of the words of a reliable person—just like memory—and because it is not contradicted by other means of valid cognition. (1833)
Furthermore, the excellence of the accounts concerning Kṛṣṇa and others has been well established by the author of the Nyāyanirṇaya in proving the superiority of the Supreme Person. (1843)

Therefore, in the *Mānameyodaya*, it is stated that whatever is true in some respect is necessarily verbal [in nature]. Consequently, the wise recognize only six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇas*). (1853)
"O Rāma! There are six methods in the world by which everything is perceived.
Thus it is also stated in the Rāmāyaṇa; therefore, all is most auspicious. (1863)
Thus ends the examination of non-existence (*abhāva*) in the section on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇapariccheda*) within the *Mānameyodaya* composed by Śrī Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa.
And the section on the means of valid cognition is completed.
